short_description: Red blood cell antigen typing, DNA, human erythrocyte antigen gene analysis of 35 antigens from 11 blood groups, utilizing whole blood, common RBC alleles reported
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0001U describes the Immucor, Inc. PreciseType® HEA Test, which is a multiplexed molecular assay on a whole blood specimen that identifies 24 polymorphisms associated with 35 human erythrocyte antigens from 11 blood groups and report of the common RBC alleles. Explanation This test uses a proprietary multiplexed molecular polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification assay of polymorphisms technology to identify the presence or absence of the selected alleles associated with a given phenotype. A separate proprietary imaging system is used to capture the fluorescent signal from individual DNA strands which is compared to a library of phenotypes. Software is used to analyze the raw data and generate assay results. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test on blood donor specimens (e.g., to identify sickle cell trait) and patients receiving transfusions to ascertain compatibility. Terminology Allele: Specific variant version of a gene at a specific locus. Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, which carry genetic information. Fluorescent: Substance which absorbs and emits light. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Polymorphisms: Literally, many forms; it can refer to variations in species or stages of development; in genetics, it refers to variations in DNA due to selection and mutation. Tips Report one unit of this code for a single specimen analyzed on a single date of service. Some payers may pay separately for collection of the specimen; check with the appropriate payer. Additional Info “U” codes are included in the CPT® code set to identify specific proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) tests. PLA codes take precedence over the usual 80000 series codes for laboratory/pathology. Use this code only for the above–described test; do not report this test using any other CPT® code. PLA code descriptors follow existing code conventions when possible, and lab techniques used include multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP), among others. guidelines: Range Specific Guideline Proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) codes describe proprietary clinical laboratory analyses and can be either provided by a single ("sole-source") laboratory or licensed or marketed to multiple providing laboratories (eg, cleared or approved by the Food and Drug Administration [FDA]). This subsection includes advanced diagnostic laboratory tests (ADLTs) and clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs), as defined under the Protecting Access to Medicare Act (PAMA) of 2014. These analyses may include a range of medical laboratory tests including, but not limited to, multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP). The descriptor nomenclature follows, where possible, existing code conventions (eg, MAAA, GSP). Unless specifically noted, even though the Proprietary Laboratory Analyses section of the code set is located at the end of the Pathology and Laboratory section of the code set, a PLA code does not fulfill Category I code criteria. PLA codes are not required to fulfill the Category I criteria. The standards for inclusion in the PLA section are: The test must be commercially available in the United States for use on human specimens and The clinical laboratory or manufacturer that offers the test must request the code. For similar laboratory analyses that fulfill Category I criteria, see codes listed in the numeric 80000 series. When a PLA code is available to report a given proprietary laboratory service, that PLA code takes precedence. The service should not be reported with any other CPT® code(s) and other CPT® code(s) should not be used to report services that may be reported with that specific PLA code. These codes encompass all analytical services required for the analysis (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization and detection). For molecular analyses, additional procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection [codes 88380 and 88381]) may be reported separately. Codes in this subsection are released on a quarterly basis to expedite dissemination for reporting. short_description: Oncology (colorectal), quantitative assessment of three urine metabolites (ascorbic acid, succinic acid and carnitine) by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) using multiple reaction monitoring acquisition, algorithm reported as likelihood of adenomatous polyps
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0002U describes the PolypDX™ test from Atlantic Diagnostic Laboratories, LLC, Metabolomic Technologies Inc., which is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA) test that uses liquid chromatography combined with tandem mass spectrometry to analyze a urine specimen for 3 specific metabolites; the test includes algorithmic analysis using patient data and the lab test results to report the patient's risk for precancerous adenomatous polyps. Explanation The test uses liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LCMS/MS) to precisely identify and determine concentration of ascorbic acid, succinic acid and carnitine metabolites in urine sample. Code 0002U also includes an algorithmic analysis, making this a Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) test that uses the LCMS/MS results and specific patient information to determine the patient's risk of having precancerous adenomatous colon polyps. Each multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis, or MAAA test, involves any analytical services to produce test results that become the raw data for the algorithmic analysis. These technical lab services may include chemical or biochemical assays; florescence in situ hybridization (FISH); and molecular pathology tests including steps such as cell lysis (using an agent or substance to break down cells into their components), extraction, amplification (making more copies of the gene), and hybridization/detection. The MAAA code also includes gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Clinicians may order this test for patients at high risk for having cancerous colon polyps due to past history or family history, which could save patients from unnecessary surgery. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; specifically for MAAAs, the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such a cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Metabolite: A substance, typically a small molecule, produced during metabolism (chemical reactions that take place in the body). Reagent: A substance used in a lab test to bring about a desired change or reaction, often to reveal the presence or quantity of another substance that is the focus of the test. short_description: Oncology (ovarian) biochemical assays of five proteins (apolipoprotein A-1, CA 125 II, follicle stimulating hormone, human epididymis protein 4, transferrin), utilizing serum, algorithm reported as a likelihood score
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0003U describes the Overa™ (OVA1 Next Generation), also called Multivariate Index Assay, 2nd Generation, (MIA2G), by Aspira Labs, Inc., Vermillion, Inc., a biochemical assay of a serum specimen to detect the presence of five biomarker proteins for ovarian cancer and includes algorithmic analysis using patient data and the lab test results to determine the patient's risk for ovarian cancer. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to test the patient’s serum for five biomarkers (apolipoprotein A–1 [APO], CA 125 II, follicle stimulating hormone [FSH], human epididymis protein 4 [HE4], and transferrin [TRF]) using an immunoassay method. The test may include various steps such as reacting the specimen with test antibodies, incubating the mixture, adding microparticles to bind the complexes to an electrode, and applying an electric charge to initiate luminescence (light–emitting) that a photomultiplier measures. The analyst reports qualitative results, indicating the presence or absence of a substance in the specimen. A proprietary algorithm is then run to combine the five biomarker results with clinical assessment into a single numerical risk score that indicates higher and lower risk for ovarian cancer. Each multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis, or MAAA test, involves any analytical services to produce test results that become the raw data for the algorithmic analysis. These technical lab services may include chemical or biochemical assays; florescence in situ hybridization (FISH); and molecular pathology tests including steps such as cell lysis (using an agent or substance to break down cells into their components), extraction, amplification (making more copies of the gene), and hybridization/detection. The MAAA code also includes gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Clinicians may order this test to determine a patient's risk for having ovarian cancer. Antibody: An immune system–related protein that can detect a harmful substance called an antigen; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; antibodies are also produced in the body in reaction to harmful organisms. Biomarker or biological marker: A measurable substance that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that detects an antibody/antigen reaction in a blood or body fluid sample, using an immunological reaction to an enzyme, or enzyme immunoassay test, or radioactively labeled substance, in a radioimmunoassay test. short_description: Oncology (prostate) gene expression profile by real-time RT-PCR of 3 genes (ERG, PCA3, and SPDEF), urine, algorithm reported as risk score
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0005U describes the ExosomeDx® Prostate (IntelliScore) from Exosome Diagnostics, Inc., which is a gene expression profiling panel, a measurement of gene activity of 3 specific genes associated with prostate cancer, on a urine specimen combined with algorithmic analysis using test results and specific patient information to report a risk score that helps the clinician manage prostate cancer. Explanation The lab analyst performs the lab tests to measure the activity of genes and express the cellular function in the form of a picture. The lab analyst also inputs the test results into a computer program to analyze the data using a specific algorithm that reports a recurrence score. Technical lab services may include gene expression profiling using highly specialized tests including real–time polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR) of the ERG, PCA3, and SPDEF genes. The analyst gathers relevant patient data, carries out a specific algorithmic analysis, and reports the results. Gene expression profiling is a tool that identifies how likely it is that early stage prostate cancer will recur after an initial treatment of surgery, for example. This helps the provider decide on the value of administering additional treatments like chemotherapy and radiation. The profiling panel measures the activity of multiple genes in cancerous cells to determine the need for further treatment. This spares the patient unnecessary treatment in some cases and gives additional treatment when a patient needs it. This a Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) test, which includes any analytical services to produce test results that become the raw data for the algorithmic analysis. These technical lab services may include chemical or biochemical assays; florescence in situ hybridization (FISH); and molecular pathology tests including steps such as cell lysis (using an agent or substance to break down cells into their components), extraction, amplification (making more copies of the gene), and hybridization/detection. The MAAA code also includes gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Chemotherapy: Cancer treatment using chemical agents and drugs. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Radiation therapy: Application of high frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors; also known as radiotherapy. short_description: Drug test(s), presumptive, with definitive confirmation of positive results, any number of drug classes, urine, includes specimen verification including DNA authentication in comparison to buccal DNA, per date of service
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0007U describes ToxProtect by Genotox Laboratories LTD, which is a presumptive urine drug screen test with confirmation of any drugs identified, plus a DNA analysis of a buccal (cheek) swab to authenticate the urine source. Explanation The test uses laboratory methods to screen for the presence of a wide range of controlled substances in urine specimens. Using a cheek swab specimen collected at the same time as the urine specimen, the lab uses genomic sequencing methods to definitively match the urine and buccal cells to ensure that the specimen is human urine taken from the intended patient. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to screen for illicit drug use, monitor medication compliance, and evaluate the presence of various drugs, over–the–counter ingredients, and metabolites, while ensuring specimen authenticity. Terminology Presumptive: A term to describe a type of test that establishes either that a substance definitely is not a specific substance, or that it probably is the specific substance; confirmatory tests commonly follow presumptive tests to establish a definitive, or certain, identification. Tips Report one unit of this code on a single date for testing a urine specimen and buccal swab to screen for any number of drug classes and authenticate the specimen. Code 0018U describes ThyraMIR by Interpace Diagnostics, which is a gene analysis of 10 micro RNA sequences from a thyroid fine needle aspirate (FNA) specimen plus an algorithmic analysis using patient data and the lab test results to report a positive or negative finding for increased thyroid cancer risk. Explanation The test uses real–time polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR) of 10 micro RNA sequences plus patient data and an algorithmic analysis, making this a Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) test. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with indeterminate thyroid nodule cytopathology results to possibly rule out thyroid cancer and avoid unnecessary thyroid surgery. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output. Cytopathology: Specialized study of cells to evaluate disease processes. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such a cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Additional Info “U” codes are included in the CPT® code set to identify specific proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) tests. PLA codes take precedence over the usual 80000 series codes for laboratory/pathology. Use this code only for the above–described test; do not report this test using any other CPT® code. PLA code descriptors follow existing code conventions when possible, and lab techniques used include multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP), among others. guidelines: Range Specific Guideline Proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) codes describe proprietary clinical laboratory analyses and can be either provided by a single ("sole-source") laboratory or licensed or marketed to multiple providing laboratories (eg, cleared or approved by the Food and Drug Administration [FDA]). This subsection includes advanced diagnostic laboratory tests (ADLTs) and clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs), as defined under the Protecting Access to Medicare Act (PAMA) of 2014. These analyses may include a range of medical laboratory tests including, but not limited to, multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP). The descriptor nomenclature follows, where possible, existing code conventions (eg, MAAA, GSP). Unless specifically noted, even though the Proprietary Laboratory Analyses section of the code set is located at the end of the Pathology and Laboratory section of the code set, a PLA code does not fulfill Category I code criteria. PLA codes are not required to fulfill the Category I criteria. The standards for inclusion in the PLA section are: The test must be commercially available in the United States for use on human specimens and The clinical laboratory or manufacturer that offers the test must request the code. For similar laboratory analyses that fulfill Category I criteria, see codes listed in the numeric 80000 series. When a PLA code is available to report a given proprietary laboratory service, that PLA code takes precedence. The service should not be reported with any other CPT® code(s) and other CPT® code(s) should not be used to report services that may be reported with that specific PLA code. These codes encompass all analytical services required for the analysis (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization and detection). For molecular analyses, additional procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection [codes 88380 and 88381]) may be reported separately. Codes in this subsection are released on a quarterly basis to expedite dissemination for reporting. See the Introduction section of the CPT® code set for a complete list of the dates of release and implementation. In order to report a PLA code, the analysis performed must fulfill the code descriptor and must be the test represented by the proprietary name listed in Appendix O. In some instances, the descriptor language of PLA codes may be identical and the code may only be differentiated by the listed proprietary name in Appendix O. When more than one PLA has an identical descriptor, the codes will be denoted by the symbol "â™“." All PLA tests will have assigned codes in the PLA section of the code set. Code 0019U describes OncoTarget and OncoTreat by DarwinHealth and Columbia University Department of Pathology and Cell Biology, which evaluates RNA gene expression in tumor activity and uses an algorithm to match those findings with the best potential therapeutic agents for the cancer. Explanation The test uses formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded or fresh tumor tissue to sequence RNA transcription genes to identify regulator proteins and uses an algorithm to match the tumor with specific effective therapeutic agents based on the findings. short_description: Targeted genomic sequence analysis panel, non-small cell lung neoplasia, DNA and RNA analysis, 23 genes, interrogation for sequence variants and rearrangements, reported as presence or absence of variants and associated therapy(ies) to consider
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0022U describes Oncomine™ Dx Target Test by Thermo Fisher Scientific, which evaluates non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or cholangiocarcinoma tumor tissue for gene sequence variants and rearrangements that might indicate possible appropriate therapies. Explanation The test evaluates non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded tumor tissue using targeted parallel gene sequencing of 23 genes to evaluate variants and rearrangements that can impact treatment options for the cancer. Clinicians may order this test to aid in selecting appropriate therapy for NSCLC patients. Terminology Formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE): A method to preserve a tissue specimen, such as a biopsy, and prepare it for microscopic examination; the process uses formalin (formaldehyde) to preserve (fix) the tissue and paraffin to embed the tissue in a waxy block that can be sliced thin for viewing on a microscope slide. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Non–small cell lung cancer: A general term that includes all types of lung cancer except for small cell lung cancer, a more aggressive form of cancer that occurs primarily in smokers and rapidly spreads to other parts of the body. Rearrangement: Alteration in gene sequence due to breakage and reattachment. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Oncology (acute myelogenous leukemia), DNA, genotyping of internal tandem duplication, p.D835, p.I836, using mononuclear cells, reported as detection or non-detection of FLT3 mutation and indication for or against the use of midostaurin
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0023U describes LeukoStrat® CDx FLT3 Mutation Assay by Invivoscribe Technologies, Inc., which is a molecular pathology test to identify mutations in the FLT3 gene to aid in treatment planning for patients with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML). Explanation The procedure first isolates mononuclear cells from the patient specimen, such as blood, then isolates and amplifies DNA using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and detects internal tandem duplication (ITD) and tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) mutations in the FLT3 gene, such as D835 and I836, if present. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) to evaluate prognosis and possible treatment options, such as midostaurin. Terminology Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. short_description: Glycosylated acute phase proteins (GlycA), nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, quantitative
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0024U describes the GlycA test for glycosylated acute phase proteins, a measure of systemic inflammation, from Laboratory Corporation of America. Explanation The lab analyst performs an analysis, typically on serum or plasma, for glycated acute phase proteins, a blood component that indicates levels of systemic inflammation. He uses nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to analyze the patient’s blood sample for proteins such as fibrinogen and other acute phase reactants associated with inflammation. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with coronary artery disease and for monitoring anti–inflammatory treatment. Unlike C–reactive protein (CRP) and other biomarkers of inflammation, GlycA combines both the protein levels and glycosylation states of multiple acute–phase proteins in serum and allows for a more stable measure of systemic inflammation with just a single test. Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR spectroscopy) uses the magnetic properties of the nucleus of an atom to identify substances and the properties of the molecule. Terminology Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Tips Report one unit of this code for a single specimen analyzed on a single date of service. Some payers may pay separately for collection of the specimen; check with the appropriate payer. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0035U only for real–time quaking–induced conversion for prion detection (RT–QuIC) from the National Prion Disease Pathology Surveillance Center. This test uses a specialized technique to detect abnormal prion proteins in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which surrounds the brain and spinal cord. The method is called real–time quaking–induced conversion (RT–QuIC), and it produces a qualitative result (positive or negative) to aid in the diagnosis of prion disease. Explanation This code represents real–time quaking–induced conversion for prion detection (RT–QuIC) from the National Prion Disease Pathology Surveillance Center. The test uses a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the clear liquid that cushions and protects the brain and spinal cord. The laboratory performs a method known as real–time quaking–induced conversion (RT–QuIC), which involves intermittent shaking cycles, to detect abnormal prion proteins. Prions are misfolded proteins that can cause neurodegenerative conditions. In RT–QuIC, the presence of abnormal prions causes normal prion protein to misfold and aggregate, producing a measurable signal. The test result is qualitative, meaning it simply indicates whether the abnormal protein is present or not. Clinicians may order this test for patients who exhibit characteristic neurodegenerative signs and symptoms of human prion disease, such as sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD), the most common form of prion disease in humans. Sporadic CJD appears spontaneously, and its cause is not known; a genetic form is very rare, and the acquired infectious form has almost been eliminated. It is believed that prion diseases occur when normal prion proteins convert (misfold) into abnormal, pathologic proteins. These diseases progress rapidly after symptoms, such as dementia, appear and are always fatal. Tips Use this code only for the appropriate proprietary test. short_description: Exome (ie, somatic mutations), paired formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue and normal specimen, sequence analyses
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0036U describes the EXaCT–1 whole exome testing from the Lab of Oncology–Molecular Detection, Weill Cornell Medicine–Clinical Genomics Laboratory, which is a molecular assay that sequences only the functional coding regions (exons), expressed as proteins, of the genome — whole exome sequencing (WES) as opposed to sequencing the entire genome. Explanation The lab analyst performs an exome gene sequence analysis to look for gene mutations that might be shared by different cancers. The procedure uses both a tumor sample (specifically, 15 unstained slides and 1 hematoxylin and eosin–stained specimen) from a prior diagnostic procedure and a matched normal sample, such as whole blood or a different type of non–tumor sample from the same patient to sequence over 20,000 genes in both healthy and malignant cells. Code 0041U describes the Lyme ImmunoBlot IgM from IGeneX Inc, which detects IgM antibodies of 5 recombinant protein groups to identify Borrelia (B.) burgdorferi, a tick–borne bacteria that causes Lyme disease. Explanation The Lyme ImmunoBlot IgM test is a qualitative immunoassay in which IgM antibodies specific to the B. burgdorferi antigens on a membrane strip are visualized. The technician performs the test on a serum specimen using ID–FISH Technology Inc.’s Lyme ImmunoBlot IgM Strips, which is a membrane strip with fixed B. burgdorferi recombinant antigens on it. Bands on the strip react to antibodies that may be present in the patient specimen for the following Borrelia burgdorferi species: B. burgdorferi B31, B. burgdorferi 297, B. californiensis, B. mayonii, B. spielmanii, B. afzelii, B. garinii, and B. valaisiana. This test is more sensitive and specific than the ELISA, IFA, or traditional Western Blot tests. It may be positive as early as 1 week after a tick bite and remain positive for six to eight weeks, or longer, after initial exposure. Clinicians may order this test for patients suspected of having Lyme disease, an inflammatory disease caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, spread by ticks, to identify the specific infectious species. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A foreign substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA): A laboratory testing method using an enzyme attached to an antigen or antibody used as a marker to detect a specific substance, such as another antigen or antibody. IgG: Immunoglobulin G is the most common type of antibody found in the blood and is a complex structure of proteins made of two heavy chains and two light chains of molecules. IgM: Immunoglobulin M is a large antibody found in the blood that is the first to appear after initial exposure to an infectious organism. Immunofluorescence assay (IFA): A technique that uses fluorescent dyes to detect the presence of antibodies bound to specific antigens usually in blood serum. Recombinant: A new gene, protein, cell, or individual that has resulted from recombination (mixing) of genes. Qualitative testing: Test to determine the presence or absence of a substance in the specimen. guidelines: Range Specific Guideline Proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) codes describe proprietary clinical laboratory analyses and can be either provided by a single ("sole-source") laboratory or licensed or marketed to multiple providing laboratories (eg, cleared or approved by the Food and Drug Administration [FDA]). This subsection includes advanced diagnostic laboratory tests (ADLTs) and clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs), as defined under the Protecting Access to Medicare Act (PAMA) of 2014. These analyses may include a range of medical laboratory tests including, but not limited to, multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP). The descriptor nomenclature follows, where possible, existing code conventions (eg, MAAA, GSP). Unless specifically noted, even though the Proprietary Laboratory Analyses section of the code set is located at the end of the Pathology and Laboratory section of the code set, a PLA code does not fulfill Category I code criteria. PLA codes are not required to fulfill the Category I criteria. The standards for inclusion in the PLA section are: The test must be commercially available in the United States for use on human specimens and The clinical laboratory or manufacturer that offers the test must request the code. For similar laboratory analyses that fulfill Category I criteria, see codes listed in the numeric 80000 series. When a PLA code is available to report a given proprietary laboratory service, that PLA code takes precedence. The service should not be reported with any other CPT® code(s) and other CPT® code(s) should not be used to report services that may be reported with that specific PLA code. These codes encompass all analytical services required for the analysis (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization and detection). For molecular analyses, additional procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection [codes 88380 and 88381]) may be reported separately. Codes in this subsection are released on a quarterly basis to expedite dissemination for reporting. See the Introduction section of the CPT® code set for a complete list of the dates of release and implementation. When more than one PLA has an identical descriptor, the codes will be denoted by the symbol "â™“." All PLA tests will have assigned codes in the PLA section of the code set. The name of the PLA test has changed in association with changes in test performance or test characteristics. The addition or modification of the therapeutic applications of the test require submission of a code change application, but it may not require a new code number.

short_description: FLT3 (fms-related tyrosine kinase 3) (eg, acute myeloid leukemia) internal tandem duplication (ITD) variants, quantitative

Report code 0046U for the FLT3 ITD MRD by NGS LabPMM LLC, an Invivoscribe Technologies, Inc., Company. The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to detect the presence of specific changes in the FMS gene for fms–related tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) over the internal tandem duplication (ITD) variants to determine the presence of minimal residual disease (MRD) in conditions such as acute myeloid leukemia. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification, to detecting and quantifying the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes. A single unit of 0046U represents next generation sequencing (NGS) testing for specific changes in the FLT3 gene known as internal tandem duplication (ITD) variants using primers, or amplification starting points. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, providers commonly order this test for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), especially those who do not show inherited genetic changes related to the condition. In these cases, called cytogenetically normal AML (CN AML), the patient may have a genetic abnormality that affects only the cells that become cancerous. This is known as a somatic mutation, meaning that the change to the gene happens during the patient’s lifetime rather than being inherited. The most common mutation found in CN AML is the FLT3 ITD mutation. Myeloid leukemia occurs when immature blood cells in the bone marrow called myeloblasts enter the blood stream or when the bone marrow produces abnormal white blood cells which then overwhelm or replace healthy blood cells and keep the blood from functioning as it should. Terminology Acute: Refers to a disease or an ailment that has a rapid onset or a short course. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Somatic mutation: Acquired, not inherited; occurring in cancer cells. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Use this code only for the appropriate proprietary test; report one unit of this code for a single specimen analyzed on a single date of service. Some payers may pay separately for collection of the specimen; check with the appropriate payer. You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. short_description: Lipoprotein, blood, high resolution fractionation and quantitation of lipoproteins, including all five major lipoprotein classes and subclasses of HDL, LDL, and VLDL by vertical auto profile ultracentrifugation
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report code 0052U for the VAP® Cholesterol Test by VAP Diagnostics Laboratory, Inc., which involves high–resolution fractionation and measures the amount of lipoprotein in a patient’s blood specimen. The test includes total lipoprotein, high–density lipoprotein (HDL), low–density lipoprotein (LDL), very–low–density lipoprotein (VLDL), lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)), intermediate–density lipoprotein (IDL), HDL subclasses (HDL2 and HDL3), LDL subclasses (LDL1, LDL2, LDL3, and LDL4), VLDL subclasses (VLDL1, VLDL2, and VLDL3), and LDL. The basic principle of the test is separation of lipoproteins based on their densities and floating rates. The lipoproteins form a rigid uniform layer at the top of the centrifuge tube after 20 to 24 hours of centrifugation, which involves spinning. The analyst adds soluble materials to raise the density of the solution containing the sample, and then spins this mixture, subjecting it to high centrifugal force, called ultracentrifugation. The various lipoproteins gather on the top of the centrifuge tube according to their densities. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to evaluate patients with atherosclerosis for an increase in the level of lipoprotein–associated phospholipase enzyme, which may further increase the risk of stroke or heart attack. This test may follow other lipoprotein tests as it provides greater specificity. Report 0068U for the MycoDART–PCR™ Dual Amplification Real–Time PCR panel for 6 Candida species, from RealTime Laboratories/MycoDART Inc., which is a rapid, amplified probe test to detect or rule out six distinct Candida (yeast) species in the patient specimen such as blood. Explanation The lab analyst processes the specimen from a direct source such as blood or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and performs amplification techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to increase the quantity of six, specific Candida–species nucleic–acid targets (C. albicans, C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. kruseii, C tropicalis, C. auris), if present. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report code 0069U for the miR–31now™, GoPath Laboratories test, which measures miR–31–3p expression in formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded colon cancer tissue, and uses an algorithm to assign an expression score to guide treatment therapy. Explanation The lab analyst processes formalin–fixed, paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tumor sample from the patient with metastatic colorectal cancer and uses quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT–qPCR) to measure miR–31–3p expression. Using the test results and patient clinical data, the procedure includes an algorithmic analysis that reports a score indicating miR–31 expression level. This procedure is a Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) test, which means that it includes both the analytical services to produce test results, and algorithmic analysis of those results (and possibly other patient data) to report a risk or prognostic score. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with wild–type RAS metastatic colon cancer (mCRC), some of whom benefit from therapy targeting epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) using medication such as cetuximab and panitumumab. short_description: Oncology (lung), mass spectrometric analysis of galectin-3-binding protein and scavenger receptor cysteine-rich type 1 protein M130, with five clinical risk factors (age, smoking status, nodule diameter, nodule-spiculation status and nodule location), utilizing plasma, algorithm reported as a categorical probability of malignancy
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0080U for the BDX–XL2 test from Biodesix®, Inc., which analyzes blood plasma for two specific proteins, the results of which are combined with five risk factors in an algorithm to determine the likelihood of a lung nodule being benign or malignant. Explanation The lab analyst processes the blood plasma and performs the technical lab steps to evaluate the specimen using mass spectrometry for two proteins, galectin–3–binding protein and scavenger receptor cysteine–rich type 1 protein M130. The lab analyst then performs a predictive algorithm using lab test results, patient risk factors such as age and smoking, and tumor characteristics such as diameter, spiculation, and location to report whether the nodule is more likely to be benign or malignant. The test includes any analytical services to produce test results that become the raw data for the algorithmic analysis. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. MCI can identify quiescent (inactive), apoptotic (dying), and necrotic (dead) regions in the tissue sample. The technician places samples of tissue from a biopsy in a multiwall plate and exposes them to various drugs. He shines LED light into the middle of the tissue, and motility contrast imaging captures the scattered light coming off and creates a 3D color image. The colors indicate the responsiveness of the cancer cells to the drugs tested. Clinicians may use the information obtained from MCI to choose chemotherapy regimens for various cancers, such as for ovarian, breast, bladder, and esophageal cancer and avoid ineffective treatments. Current chemotherapy regimens are based on a type of trial–and–error method and experience of success with certain treatments for certain cancers but are not specific to how an individual patient may respond. Many patients do not respond as expected. This test helps predict which treatments are better for individual patients. short_description: Red blood cell antigen typing, DNA, genotyping of 10 blood groups with phenotype prediction of 37 red blood cell antigens
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0084U for the BLOODchip®ID CORE XT™ test from Grifols Diagnostic Solutions Inc., which is a molecular–based assay to identify blood donor and recipient red blood cell (RBC) antigen phenotypes to help determine blood compatibility. It tests for 10 blood groups and predicts 37 human erythrocyte antigen phenotypes. Explanation This test uses a proprietary multiplexed molecular polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification assay of polymorphisms technology to identify the presence or absence of the selected alleles associated with a given phenotype (specific observable trait). Allele–specific probes attached to color–coded microspheres hybridize (combine) specifically to the labeled PCR products, and fluorescent labeling allows detection and quantification (counting) of the hybridization signal. A separate proprietary imaging system is used to capture the fluorescent signal from individual DNA strands, which is compared to a library of phenotypes. Software is used to analyze the raw data and generate assay results. The test analyzes a whole blood specimen for a total of 10 blood groups – RhCE, Kell, Kidd, Duffy, MNS, Diego, Dombrock, Colton, Cartwright, and Lutheran – for 37 RBC antigens. Clinicians order this test for patients who need repeated blood transfusions to make sure the recipient blood type and antigens are compatible with the donor. Human blood groups are classified based on the antigens on the surfaces of RBCs. There are many groups, but the primary grouping is for blood types A, B, O, and AB, depending on the presence or absence of A and B antigens. In addition to ABO incompatibility, some people develop antibodies to non–ABO antigens, such as Rh antigens, especially patients who need frequent transfusions, such as those with sickle cell anemia, who are more likely to have a transfusion reaction not only to an incompatible ABO blood type but to blood with non–ABO antigens. Terminology ABO incompatibility: An abnormal transfusion reaction between blood cells of incompatible blood types A, B, AB or O, resulting in destruction of blood cells and the formation of clumps. Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Allele: Specific variant version of a gene at a specific locus. Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A foreign substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Blood group: A set of human red blood cell antigens that can determine compatibility in transfusion; the best known groups are the ABO system and the Rh system. Erythrocyte: Also known as red blood cells (RBCs), erythrocytes contain hemoglobin, which carries oxygen throughout the body, and make up one of the three main components of blood. Fluorescent antibody test: A laboratory test in which a fluorescent agent, a substance which absorbs and emits light, is added to a specimen to detect the antigen–antibody complex using a special microscope. Genome: The entire genetic material of an organism, which means the entire DNA sequence. Genomic Sequencing Procedures (GSPs): Tests that use germline or neoplastic specimens to simultaneously analyze DNA or RNA sequences, typically for a combination of many genes or even an entire exome or genome. The tests often employ technology such as next generation sequencing (NGS) to identify changes to nucleic acid sequences or possibly other variations such as copy number or chromosomal structure, and then use bioinformatics to compare the findings to known genetic changes relevant to a specific clinical condition. Hybridization: Forming a double–stranded DNA or RNA molecule by combining two complementary single strands, usually to identify a genetic mutation. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such a cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Polymorphisms: Literally, many forms; it can refer to variations in species or stages of development; in genetics, it refers to variations in DNA due to selection and mutation. Sickle cell disease: A group of inherited red blood cell (RBC) disorders caused by an abnormal protein in the RBCs that gives the cells a curved sickle shape and results in RBC death with anemia and other complications. short_description: Gastric emptying, serial collection of 7 timed breath specimens, non-radioisotope carbon-13 (13C) spirulina substrate, analysis of each specimen by gas isotope ratio mass spectrometry, reported as rate of 13CO2 excretion
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0106U for the Cairn 13C–Spirulina Gastric Emptying Breath Test (GEBT) from Cairn Diagnostics, d/b/a Advanced Breath Diagnostics, LLC, which is a noninvasive, nonradioactive breath test that measures the rate of gastric emptying of solids in adult patients. Explanation Patients are instructed to have nothing by mouth after midnight or for at least 8 hours preceding the Cairn 13C–Spirulina Gastric Emptying Breath Test (GEBT). The collection of breath specimens and administration of the test meal are performed under the supervision of a healthcare professional, who obtains several premeal breath samples from the patient to provide a non–radioisotope carbon–13 baseline for comparison with the postmeal samples. The patient then consumes a test meal of cooked egg labeled with 13C–Spirulina platensis (a protein–rich blue–green microalgae) particles with 6 saltine crackers and 6 ounces of water. The 13C–Spirulina eventually passes from the stomach into the small intestine where it is absorbed and converted to 13C O2 and expired in the breath. Six breath samples are collected in capped glass tubes at intervals over a four–hour period beginning 45 minutes after the test meal and sent to a laboratory. In the laboratory, all pre– and postmeal breath samples are analyzed by gas isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GIRMS) to determine the ratio of 13C O2 to 12C O2. The patient’s gastric emptying rate is determined by measuring the change in this ratio and comparing it to the patient’s premeal value. A fraction over 1 percent of the food we eat contains 13C, and the remaining almost 99 percent contains 12C, so the test makes use of this information to determine whether the stomach is emptying properly. Spirulina, a nutritionally rich dietary supplement, is an edible form of blue–green microalgae given Class A safety status by the FDA and sold in the U.S. as a health food. Gastroparesis is a digestive disorder in which the stomach muscles stop functioning normally, and the stomach fails to contract and empty into the small bowel completely or at all. Patients experience symptoms of heartburn, nausea and vomiting, unstable blood glucose levels, and a feeling of fullness after meals. The most common cause of gastroparesis is diabetes, but there are other possible causes. short_description: Gastroenterology (Barrett's esophagus), whole slide-digital imaging, including morphometric analysis, computer-assisted quantitative immunolabeling of 9 protein biomarkers (p16, AMACR, p53, CD68, COX-2, CD45RO, HIF1a, HER-2, K20) and morphology, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue, algorithm reported as risk of progression to high-grade dysplasia or cancer

Report 0108U for the TissueCypher® Barrett’s Esophagus Assay from Cernostics Lab, which helps pathologists interpret esophageal biopsies and predicts the risk for high–grade dysplasia or esophageal cancer in patients with Barrett’s esophagus. short_description: Infectious disease (Aspergillus species), real-time PCR for detection of DNA from 4 species (A. fumigatus, A. terreus, A. niger, and A. flavus), blood, lavage fluid, or tissue, qualitative reporting of presence or absence of each species

Clinicians may order this test to evaluate whether a patient is at steady–state for prescription oncology drugs and whether the drug level is therapeutic (effective) or toxic (causing adverse effects). short_description: Oncology (prostate), measurement of PCA3 and TMPRSS2-ERG in urine and PSA in serum following prostatic massage, by RNA amplification and fluorescence-based detection, algorithm reported as risk score

short_description: Gastroenterology (Barrett's esophagus), VIM and CCNA1 methylation analysis, esophageal cells, algorithm reported as likelihood for Barrett's esophagus

Report 0114U for the EsoGuard™ test from Lucid Diagnostics, which uses cytosine methylation analysis of esophageal cells obtained from a swallowed balloon device and inputs the findings into an algorithm; the results are reported as the presence or absence of VIM and CCNA1 methylation, which is a predictor of Barrett’s esophagus. Explanation The patient swallows an encapsulated, expandable balloon with a textured surface in a vitamin pill–sized capsule attached to a catheter. Once the capsule is in the stomach, the balloon is everted from the capsule, inflated, and gently withdrawn 3 to 6 cm back into the esophagus where it samples the luminal epithelial lining of the esophagus. short_description: Pain management, analysis of 11 endogenous analytes (methylmalonic acid, xanthurenic acid, homocysteine, pyroglutamic acid, vanilmandelate, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, hydroxymethylglutarate, ethylmalonate, 3-hydroxypropyl mercapturic acid (3-HPMA), quinolinic acid, kynurenic acid), LC-MS/MS, urine, algorithm reported as a pain-index score with likelihood of atypical biochemical function associated with pain
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0117U for the Foundation PI test from Ethos Laboratories, which uses LC–MS/MS to evaluate a patient’s urine for metabolic compounds and metabolism breakdown products related to chronic pain. The results are incorporated along with patient data into an algorithm to provide a pain index score based on the values of biochemical markers associated with pain. Explanation The lab analyst performs quantitative test on a urine specimen using an automated analytical instrument to measure levels of certain biomarkers in the urine indicative of chronic inflammation, neurotransmitter status, nerve health, and/or oxidative stress. The instrument first passes the sample through a high–pressure liquid chromatograph to separate components, and then ionizes the components and transfers them to mass spectrometers to provide structural identity and quantification of individual components based on mass to charge ratio. This test measures the levels of methylmalonic acid (a substance related to vitamin B12 metabolism), xanthurenic acid (a compound excreted in vitamin B6 deficiency), homocysteine (an amino acid associated with B6, B12, and folate deficiencies), pyroglutamic acid (a substance that accumulates in high anion gap metabolic acidosis), vanilmandelate (breakdown products of the stress–related hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine), 5–hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5–HIAA, metabolite of the neurotransmitter serotonin) , hydroxymethylglutarate (cholesterol precursor used to make CoQ10, which enables cells to use oxygen to make energy), ethylmalonate (indicative of riboflavin deficiency and the ability to process fatty acids), 3–hydroxypropyl mercapturic acid (3–HPMA, a novel biomarker in acute spinal cord injury), and quinolinic and kynurenic acids (two substances increased in inflammatory and noninflammatory neurological disorders). An algorithmic analysis of these test results along with certain patient data provides a pain index score. Clinicians who order this test can use the result to correlate abnormal biomarker findings with non–opioid therapies to maximize the chances of success for patients on prolonged pain management regimens. short_description: Transplantation medicine, quantification of donor-derived cell-free DNA using whole genome next-generation sequencing, plasma, reported as percentage of donor-derived cell-free DNA in the total cell-free DNA
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0118U for the Viracor TRAC™ (transplant rejection allograft check) donor–derived cell–free DNA (dd–cfDNA) assay from Viracor Eurofins, which uses next generation sequencing to monitor the percentage of dd–cfDNA in transplant recipient blood following a solid organ transplant. Explanation Whole blood is collected from a patient who has undergone previous solid organ transplant in a special tube using a strict protocol and shipped to the laboratory where the lab analyst extracts the plasma and prepares it for testing. The Viracor TRAC™ dd–cfDNA assay uses automated next generation DNA sequencing to quantify the donor–derived fraction of cell–free DNA (dd–cfDNA). NGS results and genome–wide recipient genotype data (donor genotype is not needed) are then analyzed by a bioinformatics algorithm that calculates the percentage of dd–cfDNA present. Clinicians order this test for patients who have had a solid organ transplant to monitor the possibility of rejection. The percentage of dd–cfDNA strongly correlates to allograft injury due to rejection; this test avoids the need for an invasive organ biopsy. This test, however, cannot be used to determine possible transplant rejection if the donor and recipient are identical twins or siblings from parents who share blood relatives or when the patient has received multiple transplants from different donors. Solid organs include the heart, liver, kidneys, spleen, and pancreas. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0119U for the MI–HEART Ceramides, Plasma test, a Mayo Clinic Laboratory–developed test, which uses LC–MS/MS to determine levels of plasma ceramides and reports the results both quantitatively and as a risk score for serious cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction (MI), acute coronary syndrome, and death. Explanation The lab analyst performs a quantitative test on a blood plasma specimen using an automated analytical instrument to measure levels of ceramides. The instrument first passes the sample through a high–pressure liquid chromatograph to separate components, and then ionizes the components and transfers them to mass spectrometers to provide structural identity and quantification of individual components based on mass to charge ratio. The results are combined with patient data in an algorithm and reported both as measured values of ceramides and as a risk score for major cardiovascular events. Clinicians order this test for patients with or without heart disease to predict the likelihood of serious coronary events occurring within 1 to 5 years. Plasma ceramides are a family of waxy lipid (fat) molecules associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction (MI). Elevated levels of three specific ceramides (Cer16:0, Cer18:0, and Cer24:1) have been linked to plaque buildup in the arteries (atherosclerosis) and insulin resistance and indicate a higher risk of heart disease. They can help predict the need for coronary revascularization (restoration of blood supply) or hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome. Ceramide levels may also be used to predict death from heart disease within 5 years. Risk determined by plasma ceramide levels is independent of other biomarkers of heart disease such as low density lipoprotein (LDL) and C–reactive protein (CRP). short_description: Oncology (B-cell lymphoma classification), mRNA, gene expression profiling by fluorescent probe hybridization of 58 genes (45 content and 13 housekeeping genes), formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue, algorithm reported as likelihood for primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBCL) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) with cell of origin subtyping in the latter Notes: (Do not report 0120U in conjunction with 0017M)
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0120U for the Lymph3Cx Lymphoma Molecular Subtyping Assay, a Mayo Clinic Laboratory–Developed Test on a preserved biopsy tissue specimen that measures and sequences 58 genes and combines the results with patient data to determine the how likely primary mediastinal B–cell lymphoma (PMBCL) and diffuse large B–cell lymphoma (DLBCL) may occur in a patient. Explanation The specimen consists of formalin–fixed, paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue. The lab analyst performs the lab test by hybridizing (combining) fluorescent probes with specimen mRNA to provide a profile of the activity of 58 genes (45 content and 13 housekeeping). Test performance may include steps such as cell lysis, extraction, amplification, and hybridization or detection, and cell of origin subtyping for DLBCL, as well as gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results as a score to predict the likelihood of two types of lymphoma, mediastinal B–cell lymphoma (PMBCL) and diffuse large B–cell lymphoma (DLBCL). This a Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) test, which includes any analytical services to produce test results that become the raw data for the algorithmic analysis. These technical lab services may include chemical or biochemical assays; florescence in situ hybridization (FISH); and molecular pathology tests including steps such as cell lysis (using an agent or substance to break down cells into their components), extraction, amplification (making more copies of the gene), and hybridization/detection. The MAAA code also includes gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Clinicians order this test for patients with or suspected to have PMBCL or DLBCL to help decide on the value of administering additional treatments like chemotherapy and radiation. The profiling panel measures the activity of multiple genes in cancerous cells to determine the need for further treatment. short_description: Hereditary breast cancer-related disorders (eg, hereditary breast cancer, hereditary ovarian cancer, hereditary endometrial cancer), genomic sequence analysis and deletion/duplication analysis panel (ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, CHEK2, PALB2, PTEN, and TP53)
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0129U for the BRCAplus™ test from Ambry Genetics, which uses genomic sequence analysis and deletion/duplication analysis of 8 genes associated with hereditary breast cancer–related disorders. Explanation The lab analyst performs a genomic sequencing analysis panel using specialized equipment such as a next generation gene sequencer, which is an automated instrument that determines the order of nucleotides in DNA and compares the findings to a reference library of normal genomes and variant gene sequences, for 8 genes associated with hereditary breast cancer–related disorders. All 8 genes (ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, CHEK2, PALB2, PTEN, and TP53) are evaluated by next generation sequencing (NGS) or Sanger sequencing of all coding domains. NGS is used to detect the BRCA2 Portuguese founder mutation, which is confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and agarose gel electrophoresis. The analysis includes secondary sequencing method for any regions with insufficient read depth coverage for reliable heterozygous variant detection. Additional Sanger sequencing is performed to resolve variants of unknown significance when indicated. The analyst uses deletion/duplication analysis to determine whether there is an Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Gene copy number analysis by a targeted microarray identifies gross deletions and duplications. Clinicians order this test to determine whether a patient has a genetic predisposition to hereditary breast, ovarian, or endometrial cancer to modify screening practices and tailor treatment. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. The test is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analyses (MAAA that uses an algorithm to analyze the test results and possibly other patient data to report the presence or absence of minimal residual disease (MRD). Clinicians order this test for patients with myeloid malignancies to pinpoint MRD and detect mutation combinations that may impact prognosis and reoccurrence and guide treatment decisions. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body, such as the production of a specific protein. Genome: The entire genetic material of an organism, which means the entire DNA sequence. Genomic sequencing procedures (GSPs): Tests that use germline or neoplastic specimens to simultaneously analyze DNA or RNA sequences, typically for a combination of many genes or even an entire exome or genome; the tests often employ technology such as next–generation sequencing (NGS) to identify changes to nucleic acid sequences or possibly other variations, such as copy number or chromosomal structure, and then use bioinformatics to compare the findings to known genetic changes relevant to a specific clinical condition. short_description: Oncology (solid tumor as indicated by the label), somatic mutation analysis of BRCA1 (BRCA1, DNA repair associated), BRCA2 (BRCA2, DNA repair associated) and analysis of homologous recombination deficiency pathways, DNA, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue, algorithm quantifying tumor genomic instability score
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0172U for the myChoice® CDx test from Myriad Genetics Laboratories, which determines homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) status using somatic mutation analysis to detect variants in tumor suppressor genes BRCA1 and BRCA2. The test uses DNA from formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded tissues of solid organ tumors. The resulting genomic instability score provides an algorithmic measurement of certain biomarkers valuable for selection of ovarian cancer treatment. Explanation The lab analyst performs next generation sequencing–based in vitro testing using formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded tissue of solid organ tumors. The specimen undergoes multiple steps, such as fragmentation, end repair and adenylation, adapter ligation, amplification, hybridization, sequencing, and data analysis. Testing detects sequence variants and genomic rearrangements in BRCA1 and BRCA2 and analyzes genomic instability. Processes also include BRCA1 and BRCA2 variant classification, genomic instability classification, and results reporting. Clinicians may order this test for patients with ovarian cancer. A positive genomic instability calculation status (meaning test results show homologous recombination deficiency) or clinically significant variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2 supports use of certain therapies. Both BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes, and many heritable changes or mutation to these genes are associated with breast and ovarian cancer, as well as other cancers such as fallopian–tube cancer and melanoma. The BRCA gene plays a role in homologous recombination repair, which is how cells repair double–stranded DNA breaks. Mutation of this gene may lead to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), which increases genetic material instability. Oncogenesis: Transformation of normal cells into cancer cells; also called carcinogenesis. Somatic mutation: Acquired, not inherited, point mutations and small insertions and deletions occurring in cancer cells. Explanation Using a blood specimen, the lab analyst performs a high–resolution food–allergy test panel using a microarray of tiny antigen–coated beads that can react with antibodies from the patient specimen in a Luminex immunoassay to identify specific allergenic epitopes, which are small segments of food proteins that act as antigens. Antigen: A foreign substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Explanation BioFire® FilmArray® Respiratory Panel 2.1 is an automated laboratory panel that generates a result of “detected” or “not detected” for 22 respiratory pathogens in a single report, including SARS–CoV–2. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0203U describes the PredictSURE IBD™ Test by PredictImmune Ltd. and KSL Diagnostics. The test is a quantitative RT–PCR test using whole blood from a patient. The results help guide clinical management of aggressive types of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) such as Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. Explanation The lab analyst performs the test using a whole blood specimen to quantitatively measure the activity of 17 genes using real time (quantitative) reverse–transcription polymerase chain reaction (quantitative RT–PCR), which monitors amplification of targeted mRNA gene expression. The test includes analyzing the data using a specific algorithm to report results as a percentage risk for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) aggressiveness, such as “high–risk, with 95% probability that they are in the high–risk subgroup.” Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with a new IBD diagnosis to determine if the patient is likely to experience an aggressive or milder form of the disease. Inflammatory bowel disease is a condition that may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, causing inflammation of the lining of the digestive tract; symptoms include abdominal pain, persistent diarrhea, loss of weight, tiredness, and sometimes rectal bleeding; Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are severe forms of IBD. The results are reported as a continuous risk score and classification of IBD aggressiveness, which can help clinicians and patients determine the best course of monitoring or treatment action. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Reverse transcription: Generation of a complementary DNA sequence from a template of RNA. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0205U describes the Vita Risk® test by Arctic Medical Laboratories, which reveals whether a patient has an increased risk of progressing from dry to wet age–related macular degeneration (AMD) if they take zinc supplements. Explanation The lab analyst prepares the specimen taken by buccal swab (a smear from the inner cheek). He performs the test using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and matrix–assisted laser desorption/ionization–time of flight (MALDI–TOF) to identify three gene variants, two in the complement factor H (CFH) gene and one in the age–related maculopathy susceptibility 2 (ARMS2) gene. A genetic profile with two CFH risk variants and an absence of risk markers at ARMS2 indicates increased risk associated with zinc supplements. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to identify patients with dry AMD who have an increased risk of progression to wet AMD after chronic exposure to zinc. The clinician can use the results to inform patients about whether zinc supplements may be beneficial or may increase risk of vision loss. Many patients with dry AMD take a supplement that includes zinc because of studies indicating the supplement may help slow the progression of AMD. AMD is weakening of a small area in the retina, the macula, that leads to vision loss in people age 50 or older. Dry macular degeneration does not involve the bleeding or leaking blood vessels that characterize wet macular degeneration. short_description: Neurology (Alzheimer disease); cell aggregation using morphometric imaging and protein kinase C-epsilon (PKCe) concentration in response to amylospheroid treatment by ELISA, cultured skin fibroblasts, each reported as positive or negative for Alzheimer disease
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0206U describes the Discern™ test by NeuroDiagnostics. The analyst subjects a cultured skin specimen to assay measurements for morphometric imaging and protein kinase C–epsilon (PKCe) biomarkers to identify Alzheimer disease. Explanation The lab analyst prepares a small skin sample by incubating it for a few weeks to reach threshold volumes of more than 1,000,000 cells. For the morphometric imaging assay biomarker, the analyst stimulates the cultured skin specimen with an extracellular matrix that forms networks in control and non–Alzheimer disease cells, but not in Alzheimer disease (AD) cells. The network formation is quantified and helps in diagnosis of AD. For the protein kinase C–epsilon (PKCe) biomarker, the lab analyst uses the cultured skin specimen with PKCe–specific antibodies to quantify relative levels of PKCe to identify and differentiate between AD and non–AD dementia. Amylospheroid is an assembly of amyloid beta peptides that can induce death in functionally mature neurons and cause AD and dementia. The changes in morphometric imaging and PKCe concentration in response to amylospheroid treatment by ELISA may indicate AD. The test results are reported either as positive or negative for AD. Clinicians may order this test to detect AD and differentiate it from other dementias. AD is a slowly progressive form of dementia characterized by beta–amyloid plaques (microscopic clumps of pieces of protein), tangles (strands) of the tau protein (abundant in the central nervous system but not elsewhere), brain inflammation, and damage and eventual death of brain cells. The characteristic symptoms of dementia are loss of memory, language, problem–solving, and other cognitive skills that affect a person’s activities of daily living. Terminology Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Dementia: Forgetfulness associated with at least one other cognitive disorder, such as language disorder, the inability to carry out purposeful movement unrelated to physical impairment, recognize or respond appropriately to sensory stimuli, plan or organize activities, or think abstractly. Enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA): A laboratory testing method using an enzyme attached to an antigen or antibody used as a marker to detect a specific substance, such as another antigen or antibody. Extracellular matrix (ECM): Material secreted by cells that provides a supportive framework for surrounding cells.
