Analysis of the whole genome and mitochondrial DNA provides data for evaluating rare, unexplained constitutional or genetic disorders in a proband patient (the first patient in a family to receive the genetic testing). Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood or saliva, the lab analyst performs a single platform test to analyze the whole genome sequence (WGS), constitutional genome–wide copy number variation (CNV), gene tandem repeat expansion, and mitochondrial whole genome sequence with deletion/duplication and heteroplasmy (cells with mitochondrial DNA mutations in some, but not all, mitochondria). Testing is for the proband, the first person in a family to get genetic counseling or testing for a possible genetic disorder. The procedure involves using specialized equipment such as a next generation sequencer, which is an automated instrument that determines the order of nucleotides in DNA. Proprietary algorithms analyze the data, which is interpreted by an analyst in relation to the patient’s physical characteristics. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Red cell antigen (ABO blood group) genotyping (ABO), gene analysis, next-generation sequencing, ABO (ABO, alpha 1-3-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase and alpha 1-3-galactosyltransferase) gene
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0221U for the Navigator ABO Blood Group NGS test from Grifols Immunohematology Center using a specimen such as blood. Analysis of the specific gene sequences listed in the code indicates ABO blood group antigens, which may help clinicians minimize adverse blood–type incompatibility reactions in blood transfusions, organ transplants, or in pregnancy and newborns. Explanation The lab analyst performs gene analysis using a patient specimen such as blood or saliva to analyze differences in the ABO (ABO, alpha 1–3–N–acetylgalactosaminyltransferase and alpha 1–3–galactosyltransferase) gene. Variation in the ABO gene determines the individual’s ABO blood group by determining the presence or absence of specific red blood cell (RBC) antigens. The test uses next generation sequencing (NGS) to identify genetic markers for specific red blood cell antigens in the ABO blood group. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA nucleotides in many genes. The instrument identifies each sequence as a string of letters, called a read, and compares the sequences to a library of normal and variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test on specimens from blood or tissue donors and recipients to improve transfusion or transplant compatibility, or on specimens from maternal blood to minimize newborn adverse blood reactions or maternal antibody formation. ABO is the most common blood group system producing familiar blood types A, B, AB, and O. Blood group genotyping provides some advantages over traditional serology typing methods, which may be compromised by antibody interference, or weak antibody reactivity or antigen expression. Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Antigen: A foreign substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Blood group: A set of human red blood cell antigens that can determine compatibility in transfusion; the best known groups are the ABO system and the Rh system. Exon: Nucleic acid sequence that includes at least part of the code for a specific product, such as a protein. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Red blood cells (RBCs): One of three primary cell types in blood that primarily carries oxygen through the body on the hemoglobin molecule; the red–colored protein in the red blood cell that carries oxygen to the tissue and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs; RBCs have surface antigens that can form antibodies, typically through exposure via pregnancy or blood transfusion; at a future time, these antibodies can cause hemolytic anemia, killing fetal RBCs during pregnancy, or transfused RBCs during a blood transfusion, or possibly the patient's own RBCs due to an autoimmune response; also known as erythrocytes. Explanation QIAstat–Dx® Respiratory SARS CoV–2 Panel is an automated laboratory panel that generates a result of “detected” or “not detected” for 22 respiratory pathogens in a single report, including SARS–CoV–2. The lab analyst receives the nasopharyngeal swab specimen in transport media, and processes the sample using a QIAstat–Dx® Respiratory SARS CoV–2 Panel, which is an automated multiplex PCR analyzer that incorporates sample preparation, nucleic acid amplification, target detection, analysis, and reporting in a single platform. Clinicians order this test for patients with respiratory infection symptoms to detect and differentiate nucleic acid of SARS–CoV–2, the organism that causes COVID–19, from multiple other common respiratory viral and bacterial pathogens. QIAstat–Dx® Respiratory SARS CoV–2 Panel test is authorized by the FDA under the Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for use by authorized laboratories for the duration of the COVID–19 emergency declaration. Terminology Bacteria (sing. bacterium): Single–celled microorganisms visible only with a microscope, some of which cause infection. COVID–19: Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID–19) is a disease caused by a novel coronavirus, SARS–CoV–2, that resulted in declaration of a global pandemic beginning in March 2020. short_description: Hepcidin-25, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), serum or plasma
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report code 0251U for Intrinsic Hepcidin IDxTM Test from Intrinsic LifeSciencesTM LLC, which is an enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) using a monoclonal antibody that binds to hepcidin in the serum or plasma specimen to evaluate hepcidin levels for clinical applications related to iron therapy. Explanation Using a serum or plasma specimen, the lab analyst performs an enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to evaluate the level of hepcidin, which helps regulate dietary iron absorption, iron transport, and iron recycling from dying red blood cells. The assay uses a monoclonal antibody that binds to the N–terminus of hepcidin–25 and some less common hepcidin isomers. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with iron deficiency anemia associated with conditions such as chronic kidney disease, some cancers, and rheumatoid arthritis, to help predict response to oral iron therapy. The test uses tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) to measure the levels of VLCAD enzyme activity in leukocytes to aid in diagnosis and treatment planning for VLCAD deficiency, which is a severe disorder of fatty–acid metabolism. Explanation Using a blood specimen, the lab analyst isolates leukocytes, which are white blood cells, and uses a procedure such as tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), which ionizes, separates, fragments, and detects targets in the specimen based on mass, to determine the level of Very–Long Chain Acyl–CoA Dehydrogenase (VLCAD) enzyme in the specimen. VLCAD deficiency may result in severe conditions impacting multiple organs that could be progressive and fatal, but early intervention can improve outcomes. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to evaluate gene expression of 50 to 100 genes and algorithmic analysis of the findings to aid in selecting appropriate medication to treat psoriasis. Explanation Using RNA captured from a proprietary Mindera patch applied to a psoriasis lesion, the lab analyst uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to evaluate gene expression, which is RNA transcription from DNA, of 50 to 100 genes that includes over 7000 biomarkers. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes from the patient specimen and use bioinformatics to interpret the results relative to variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. The assay includes an algorithmic analysis of the findings using the Mindera SkinAtlas™ database to target patient response to treatment medications. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to aid in selection of the most successful psoriasis treatment option for the individual. Current psoriasis treatment often requires multiple changes in medication to find the most successful option, adding to patient discomfort and expense. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA m(RNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing Nucleotide: A compound or organic molecule that forms the basic structural unit of nucleic acids, such as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). Transcription: Generation of complementary mRNA sequence from a DNA template. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0259U only for GFR by NMR, from Labtech™ Diagnostics, on a serum specimen. The test uses nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to measure myo–inositol, valine, and creatinine, plus an immunoassay to measure cystatin C. Using the test results and demographic data, an algorithmic analysis produces an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which indicates how well the kidneys are working, specifically for patients with chronic kidney disease. Explanation The lab analyst measures the serum level of a group of metabolites including myo–inositol, valine, and creatinine using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, which can identify and quantify molecules based on magnetic properties of the nuclei of atoms. The analyst also performs an immunoassay that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to measure cystatin C levels in the serum, and combines the findings with patient data and an algorithmic analysis to determine an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with chronic kidney disease to indicate how well the kidneys are functioning. Specifically, GFR indicates the rate at which blood passes through the kidney filter clusters, called glomeruli. Standard testing for estimated GFR uses blood creatinine levels, but recent studies indicate the NMR method provides a better estimate of GFR. Terminology Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as by producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR): The rate at which the kidneys can process the elements in the blood so they can be eliminated through urine. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Metabolite: A chemical used or made as part of processes in the body, called metabolism, that make energy and substances for living and functioning. Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR spectroscopy): A technique that uses magnetic properties of the nucleus of an atom to identify substances and the properties of the molecule. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. The test, on a specimen such as blood, uses optical genome mapping (OGM) to identify chromosomal structural variants to aid in diagnosis of neurodevelopmental genetic disorders. Explanation The lab analyst performs optical genomic mapping (OGM), which offers a high–resolution view of the structural organization of chromosomes and DNA. OGM focuses on identifying and mapping structural variations in the genome, such as copy number variations, inversions, insertions, deletions, and translocations. The single assay provides similar data typically available using different assays, such as chromosomal microarray, Fragile X testing, and karyotyping. Clinicians may order this test to aid in diagnosis and treatment of patients with suspected neurodevelopmental genetic disorders. Neurodevelopmental disorders are a group of disorders associated with delayed or impaired brain and/or central nervous system development resulting in developmental brain dysfunction, impaired motor function, and mental disorders. Terminology Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Fragile X syndrome: A genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the FMR1 gene, resulting in intellectual disability and certain facial characteristics. Heritable: Refers to the variance of a genetic trait as it's expressed in a population, i.e., a certain genetic trait be expressed 80% of the time, 60% of the time, or 30% of the time; inheritable simply means that a certain trait, such a color of eyes or hair, is genetic. Karyotyping: A lab test that pairs all chromosomes of an organism to reveal number and structural features that could indicate genetic anomalies. Rearrangement: Alteration in gene sequence due to breakage and reattachment. Translocation: The process or genetic abnormality that occurs when disparate portions of one or more chromosomes become attached and create a hybrid segment, known as a fusion gene, inserted in one or both of the broken chromosomes. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Oncology (colorectal cancer), image analysis with artificial intelligence assessment of 4 histologic and immunohistochemical features (CD3 and CD8 within tumor-stroma border and tumor core), tissue, reported as immune response and recurrence-risk score
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0261U only for Immunoscore®, from HalioDx, on a formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) colon cancer tissue specimen. The test uses digital assessment of CD3 and CD8, which indicate immune response to the tumor, to report a score for immune response and a score for risk–of–recurrence as high or low. Clinicians may order the test for patients with localized colon cancer to guide treatment. Explanation The lab analyst performs digital analysis of microscopic images of a formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) colon cancer tissue specimen. The analyst specifically targets the digital imaging to determine levels of CD3 and CD8, which are T–cell co–receptors, to measure host immune response at the tumor border and core. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with localized colon cancer. Compared to typical diagnostic tools to define tumor cell characteristics (histopathology) and to assess relevant genetic mutations, this test uniquely evaluates the body’s immune response to the tumor, and is a strong indicator of treatment outcomes. The test results indicate the level of CD3 and CD8 as an immune–response score (IS 0–4) and a risk–of–relapse score of “High” (for IS 0 and 1) or “Low” (for IS 2–4). Terminology CD3: A specific protein complex co–receptor that works with T–cell receptors to facilitate an immune response. CD8: A specific transmembrane protein co–receptor that works with T–cell receptors to facilitate an immune response. Co–receptor: A cell–surface molecule that helps bind a cell to a specific receptor to facilitate a biological process. T–cell: A type of white blood cells, also called T–lymphocytes, that facilitate the body’s immune response against infection and cancer. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0264U only for Praxis Optical Genome Mapping from Praxis Genomics LLC. The test, on a specimen such as blood, uses optical genome mapping (OGM) to identify chromosomal structural variants to aid in diagnosis of genetic disorders. Explanation The lab analyst performs optical genomic mapping (OGM), which offers a high–resolution view of the structural organization of chromosomes and DNA. OGM focuses on identifying and mapping structural variations in the genome, such as copy number variations, inversions, insertions, deletions, and translocations. The single assay provides similar data typically available using different assays, such as chromosomal microarray, Fragile X testing, and karyotyping. Clinicians may order this test to aid in diagnosis and treatment of patients with suspected genetic disorders. Terminology Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Fragile X syndrome: A genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the FMR1 gene, resulting in intellectual disability and certain facial characteristics. Heritable: Refers to the variance of a genetic trait as it's expressed in a population, i.e., a certain genetic trait be expressed 80% of the time, 60% of the time, or 30% of the time; inheritable simply means that a certain trait, such a color of eyes or hair, is genetic. Karyotyping: A lab test that pairs all chromosomes of an organism to reveal number and structural features that could indicate genetic anomalies. Rearrangement: Alteration in gene sequence due to breakage and reattachment. Translocation: The process or genetic abnormality that occurs when disparate portions of one or more chromosomes become attached and create a hybrid segment, known as a fusion gene, inserted in one or both of the broken chromosomes. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. These analyses may include a range of medical laboratory tests including, but not limited to, multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP). The descriptor nomenclature follows, where possible, existing code conventions (eg, MAAA, GSP). Unless specifically noted, even though the Proprietary Laboratory Analyses section of the code set is located at the end of the Pathology and Laboratory section of the code set, a PLA code does not fulfill Category I code criteria. PLA codes are not required to fulfill the Category I criteria. The standards for inclusion in the PLA section are: The test must be commercially available in the United States for use on human specimens and The clinical laboratory or manufacturer that offers the test must request the code. For similar laboratory analyses that fulfill Category I criteria, see codes listed in the numeric 80000 series. When a PLA code is available to report a given proprietary laboratory service, that PLA code takes precedence. The service should not be reported with any other CPT® code(s) and other CPT® code(s) should not be used to report services that may be reported with that specific PLA code. These codes encompass all analytical services required for the analysis (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization and detection). For molecular analyses, additional procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection [codes 88380 and 88381]) may be reported separately. Codes in this subsection are released on a quarterly basis to expedite dissemination for reporting. PLA codes will be published electronically on the AMA CPT® website (ama-assn.org/cpt-pla-codes), distributed via CPT® data files on a quarterly basis, and, at a minimum, made available in print annually in the CPT® codebook. See the Introduction section of the CPT® code set for a complete list of the dates of release and implementation. All codes that are included in this section are also included in Appendix O, with the procedure's proprietary name. In order to report a PLA code, the analysis performed must fulfill the code descriptor and must be the test represented by the proprietary name listed in Appendix O. In some instances, the descriptor language of PLA codes may be identical and the code may only be differentiated by the listed proprietary name in Appendix O. When more than one PLA has an identical descriptor, the codes will be denoted by the symbol "â™“." All PLA tests will have assigned codes in the PLA section of the code set. Any PLA coded test(s) that satisfies Category I criteria and has been accepted by the CPT® Editorial Panel will be designated by the addition of the symbol "^" to the existing PLA code and will remain in the PLA section of the code set. If a proprietary test has already been accepted for a Category I code and a code has not been published, subsequent application for a PLA code will take precedence. The code will only be placed in the PLA section. The accuracy of a PLA code is to be maintained by the original applicant, or the current owner of the test kit or laboratory performing the proprietary test. A new PLA code is required when: 1. Additional nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and/or protein analysis(es) are added to the current PLA test, or 2. The name of the PLA test has changed in association with changes in test performance or test characteristics. short_description: Hematology (congenital neutropenia), genomic sequence analysis of 24 genes, blood, buccal swab, or amniotic fluid
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0271U only for Versiti™ Congenital Neutropenia Panel from Versiti™ Diagnostic Laboratories using a specimen such as blood, buccal swab, or amniotic fluid. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) analysis of 24 genes associated with congenital neutropenia and may aid clinicians in diagnosing symptomatic patients or evaluating familial risk for inherited conditions. Explanation The lab analyst performs genomic sequence analysis using a patient specimen such as blood, buccal (cheek) swab, or amniotic fluid to detect genetic variation associated with congenital neutropenia. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to identify possible genetic variation in 24 genes. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA nucleotides in many genes from the patient specimen and use bioinformatics to interpret the results relative to variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. Clinicians may order this test to detect genetic variants related to congenital neutropenia, which is a condition present from birth characterized by recurrent infections due to low levels of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell important in fighting infection and inflammation. Clinicians may order the test to aid in clinical diagnosis or to evaluate familial risk for inherited conditions. Terminology Amniotic fluid: The fluid within the amniotic sac that surrounds the fetus and helps to protect it from mechanical injury. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Buccal: Pertaining to the inside of the cheeks. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Neutropenia: Decreased numbers of neutrophils, the most abundant form of white blood cells in the blood; neutrophils originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, are short–lived, and are essential to the functioning of the immune system. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Nucleotide: A compound or organic molecule that forms the basic structural unit of nucleic acids, such as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Use this code only for the appropriate proprietary test; report one unit of this code for a single specimen analyzed on a single date of service. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. Additional Info “U” codes are included in the CPT® code set to identify specific proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) tests. PLA codes take precedence over the usual 80000 series codes for laboratory/pathology. Use this code only for the above–described test; do not report this test using any other CPT® code. PLA code descriptors follow existing code conventions when possible, and lab techniques used include multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP), among others. Report 0273U only for Versiti™ Fibrinolytic Disorder Panel from Versiti™ Diagnostic Laboratories using a specimen such as blood, buccal swab, or amniotic fluid. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) analysis of eight genes plus array Comparative Genomic Hybridization (aCGH) of one gene to aid in diagnosis of symptomatic patients or evaluation of familial risk for delayed bleeding disorders caused by hyperfibrinolysis. Explanation The lab analyst evaluates a patient specimen such as blood, buccal swab, or amniotic fluid to detect genetic variation associated with genetic bleeding disorders characterized by hyperfibrinolysis and delayed bleeding. Clinicians may order this test to aid in diagnosis and appropriate therapeutic intervention for patients with delayed bleeding following events such as surgery, dental work, or venipuncture, or to aid in familial risk assessment for inherited conditions. short_description: Hematology (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia), platelet antibody reactivity by flow cytometry, serum
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0275U only for Versiti™ Heparin–Induced Thrombocytopenia Evaluation – PEA, from Versiti™ Diagnostic Laboratories using a serum specimen for the platelet P–selectin expression assay (PEA) by flow cytometry to detect heparin–dependent platelet antibodies. The test can aid in the diagnosis of Heparin–Induced Thrombocytopenia/Thrombosis (HIT or HITT). short_description: Oncology, disease progression and response monitoring to radiation, chemotherapy, or other systematic cancer treatments, cell-free DNA, quantitative branched chain DNA amplification, plasma, reported in ng/mL
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0285U only for RadTox™ cfDNA test from DiaCarta Inc. The test analyzes a plasma specimen for certain cell–free DNA sequences and reports the result in ng/mL to help the provider monitor disease progression and response in a patient undergoing cancer treatment. Explanation This code represents RadTox™ cfDNA test from DiaCarta Inc. Using a plasma specimen (the liquid that remains after removing blood cells), the lab analyst performs quantitative branched chain DNA amplification. This method measures the amount of specific DNA or RNA in a sample. Instead of copying the genetic material itself, it uses special branched DNA probes that attach to the target and build a signal amplification system. This produces a light signal, and the brightness of the light shows how much of the target is present. The more light there is, the more target DNA or RNA there is. In this case, the process allows quantification of the level of target cell–free DNA (cfDNA) in the patient specimen. The test reports the results in ng/mL. A nanogram (ng) is one–billionth of a gram. Providers may use the test to track cancer progression and monitor how a tumor responds to treatment. The test directly measures the concentration of cfDNA, which can increase when cancer cells are damaged or die. This test helps monitor changes in cfDNA levels during treatments like radiation therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and other cancer therapies. The test evaluates paired normal and malignant (tumor) specimens from the patient, such as blood, bone marrow, or fresh or formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to identify DNA sequence changes, such as single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and copy number variants (CNVs) such as insertions and deletions (indels), between the normal and tumor (somatic) tissue. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Formalin: Diluted formaldehyde used to preserve biologic tissue for laboratory analysis. Somatic mutation: Acquired, not inherited, point mutations and small insertions and deletions occurring in cancer cells. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Oncology (pan tumor), whole genome optical genome mapping of paired malignant and normal DNA specimens, fresh frozen tissue, blood, or bone marrow, comparative structural variant identification
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0299U only for Praxis Somatic Optical Genome Mapping from Praxis Genomics LLC. The test evaluates paired normal and malignant (tumor) specimens from the patient such as blood, bone marrow, or frozen tissue. The test uses optical genome mapping (OGM) to compare large segments of DNA from the normal and malignant specimens to identify structural changes such as chromosomal rearrangement and repetitive or rearranged DNA regions that could be associated with the patient’s cancer. Explanation The lab analyst performs optical genomic mapping (OGM) using the Saphyr® System from Bionano Genomics Inc. The method compares DNA from paired normal and malignant (tumor) specimens from the patient such as blood, bone marrow, or frozen tissue, specifically evaluating large–scale structural changes in DNA, such as large repeated, translocated, inverted, or deleted DNA sequences or rearrangement of chromosome segments. The method creates a unique “barcode” for large, fluorescently marked DNA segments, and then uses overlapping regions of the segments to create a genome–wide barcode, which is effectively an image of the genome. By comparing the normal– and malignant–specimen barcodes, the method allows optical evaluation of large structural changes in the genome. Clinicians may order this test to aid in identifying large structural cytogenetic variants that could be associated with the patient’s cancer. Terminology Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Cytogenetics: Genetic studies related to structural variation of chromosomes. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Rearrangement: Alteration in gene sequence due to breakage and reattachment. Somatic mutation: Acquired, not inherited, point mutations and small insertions and deletions occurring in cancer cells. short_description: Oncology (minimal residual disease [MRD]), next-generation targeted sequencing analysis, cell-free DNA, initial (baseline) assessment to determine a patient-specific panel for future comparisons to evaluate for MRD Notes: (Do not report 0306U in conjunction with 0307U)
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0306U only for Invitae PCM Tissue Profiling and MRD Baseline Assay from Invitae Corporation. The test maps the DNA sequence of a tumor specimen to develop a tumor profile that serves as the baseline for subsequent testing to determine minimal residual disease (MRD), which is the level of cancer cells in the blood following treatment. Explanation Using a tumor specimen from a patient undergoing treatment for cancer, the lab analyst uses Invitae’s Anchored Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), called AMP™, to sequence the cancer DNA as a baseline for further testing. The procedure uses error–corrected next–generation sequencing (NGS) to identify changes to nucleic acid sequences or possibly other variations such as copy number or chromosomal structure, and then uses bioinformatics to compare the findings to known genetic changes relevant to the patient’s cancer. The test evaluates the entire cancer exome, which are the DNA sequences actively involved in producing proteins. After the lab performs this test to create a tumor profile, the clinician can sample patient blood and perform a separate test (0307U) to identify small quantities of tumor DNA circulating in blood, called circulating tumor (ct)DNA. ctDNA is a biomarker for minimal residual disease (MRD). The clinician may use the test results to determine whether the patient needs adjuvant cancer therapy and may use subsequent tests to monitor whether cancer returns. The ctDNA test can identify relapse earlier than imaging diagnostics can. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Cell–free DNA (cfDNA): Nonencapsulated DNA in the form of nucleic acid fragments that enter the bloodstream during apoptosis (programmed, or normal, cell death) or necrosis (cell death due to loss of blood supply from injury, radiation, or chemicals). Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Circulating–tumor DNA (ctDNA): DNA that comes from a tumor and circulates in the blood; a specific type of cell–free DNA. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Exome: Portion of the genome made up of exons, which are DNA sequences that transcribe to mature RNA, also known as mature messenger RNA (mRNA), which remains in cells and produces proteins through a process known as translation; the human exome constitutes about 1% to 2% of the human genome. Minimal residual disease (MRD): Low level of cancer cells remaining in the body following cancer treatment. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Relapse: Recurrence of a disease or condition after treatment and temporary improvement. MIC refers to the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial agent (such as an antibiotic) that inhibits microorganism (such as bacteria) growth. short_description: Autoimmune diseases (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE]), analysis of 8 IgG autoantibodies and 2 cell-bound complement activation products using enzyme-linked immunosorbent immunoassay (ELISA), flow cytometry and indirect immunofluorescence, serum, or plasma and whole blood, individual components reported along with an algorithmic SLE-likelihood assessment
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0312U to be reported only for Avise® Lupus from Exagen, Inc. Using a specimen such as serum, or plasma and whole blood, the test identifies 10 biomarkers to aid in the differential diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The biomarkers include eight IgG autoantibodies associated with SLE and two cell–bound complement activation products (CB–CAPs). CB–CAPs are traces of cell–surface proteins activated as part of the complement immune system, which is the body’s first line of defense against foreign invaders. Explanation Using a specimen such as serum, or plasma and whole blood, the test identifies 10 biomarkers for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The test uses flow cytometry to identify C4d fragments bound to erythrocytes (EC4d) and B–lymphocytes (BC4d); C4d is a degradation product of the complement immune pathway that is the body’s first line of defense against foreign invaders. The test also uses immunoassay methods to identify eight autoantibodies associated with SLE, such as anti–neutrophil antibody (ANA). This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results as raw data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Avise® Lupus reports the results of each of the 10 biomarkers and uses an algorithmic analysis of those results to identify the patient as negative, indeterminate, or positive for SLE. Clinicians often order ANA as an initial test for autoimmune connective tissue disorders, but the test doesn’t distinguish between specific forms. The Avise® Lupus test may be a useful second–tier test for ANA positive patients to aid in differential diagnosis of SLE. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Complement pathway: Part of the immune response that involves circulating proteins in plasma. Erythrocyte: Also known as red blood cells (RBCs), erythrocytes contain hemoglobin, which carries oxygen throughout the body, and make up one of the three main components of blood. Flow cytometry: A laboratory test in which a stream of stained or fluorescently marked blood cells are suspended in fluid in an electronic detector (flow cytometer); the cells travel in a single line past a focused light or laser beam that causes the stained cells to fluoresce and scatter light according to their DNA and nuclear structure; the fluorescence and light scatter are measured with a photodetector and analyzed; this test can be used to identify antigens and cancer cells as well as for staging. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): An autoimmune disease of the connective tissues in which the body attacks itself, resulting in damage to organs, joints, and other tissues; often also resulting in inflammation of the skin. short_description: Oncology (pancreas), DNA and mRNA next-generation sequencing analysis of 74 genes and analysis of CEA (CEACAM5) gene expression, pancreatic cyst fluid, algorithm reported as a categorical result (ie, negative, low probability of neoplasia or positive, high probability of neoplasia)
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0313U only for PancreaSeq® Genomic Classifier from University of Pittsburgh Medical Center Molecular and Genomic Pathology Laboratory. Using fluid from a pancreatic cyst identified by imaging, the test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) analysis of 74 genes and gene [removed]RNA) analysis of a gene known as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) or carcinoembryonic antigen–related cell adhesion molecule 5 (CEACAM5), which is a biomarker for gastrointestinal cancers. Using an algorithmic analysis of the results, the test provides a probability score of negative (low probability) or positive (high probability) that the cyst harbors genetic changes that could lead to cancer. Explanation Using a specimen such as endoscopic ultrasound fine needle aspirate (EUS–FNA) from a pancreatic cyst, the lab analyst uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to interrogate 74 genes. The test allows detection of relevant mutations such as single nucleotide variants (SNVs), insertions and deletions (indels), loss of heterozygosity (LOH), and copy number variants (CNVs) relevant to pancreatic cyst progression to cancer. The test also uses quantitative reverse transcriptase–polymerase chain reaction (qRT–PCR) to detect gene expression of the carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) gene, also known as carcinoembryonic antigen–related cell adhesion molecule 5 (CEACAM5). The CEA DNA is expressed by acting as a template for RNA in a process called transcription, then the RNA acts to produce the CEA protein in a process called translation. CEA protein is a specific marker for gastrointestinal cancer. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results as raw data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. PancreaSeq® Genomic Classifier uses the lab test genetic findings in an algorithmic analysis to report negative or positive findings for pancreatic cyst types: benign (such as serous cystadenomas), mucinous (IPMN/MCN), or cystic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs). The report also indicates the of risk of progression to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas. Clinicians may use the findings for prognosis and treatment indications. Terminology Adenocarcinoma: Cancer that begins in glandular cells. Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using a lighted tubular instrument with attached camera specially designed for the procedure; endoscopies include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal (digestive) tract, the urinary system, the upper respiratory system, and the eye. Fine needle aspiration (FNA): A technique to obtain fluid, tissue, and/or cell samples for laboratory analysis by sucking (aspirating) them up into a syringe attached to a needle of very fine diameter inserted into the target area. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Neuroendocrine tumors: Abnormal masses that originate from cells of the endocrine or nervous system, commonly occur in the intestines, but may also be found in the lung and other parts of the body. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Nucleotides: Biochemicals — sometimes called “bases” — that form the building blocks of nucleic acids, DNA and RNA; DNA is made up of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T), while RNA uses uracil (U) in place of T; each base will pair with only one specific “complementary” base when forming DNA or RNA strands. short_description: Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), OspA protein evaluation, urine
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0316U only for Lyme Borrelia Nanotrap® Urine Antigen Test from Galaxy Diagnostics Inc. The test uses specialized nanoparticles (Nanotrap®) to capture outer surface protein A (OspA) present in urine of patients infected with Borrelia species, the organisms that cause Lyme disease. Following sample enrichment to ensure detection of small quantities of OspA, the test uses the Western blot lab procedure to quantify the protein as an indicator of active infection. Explanation The lab analyst processes a urine specimen from a patient with suspected Lyme disease, capturing any outer surface protein A (OspA) using specialized nanoparticles (Nanotrap®). OspA is present in urine of patients infected with Borrelia species, the organisms that cause Lyme disease. The analyst then performs a sample enrichment step that may concentrate OspA up to 10,000–fold to ensure detection of even a small amount of the protein in urine. Using sensitive Western blot equipment, the lab analyst applies an electrical field across a gel containing the specimen to separate protein fractions, then transfers the proteins to a membrane in a process called blotting, to quantify the level of OspA in the specimen. Presence of OspA confirms active infection with Borrelia species. Clinicians may order this test as a direct detection method for Borrelia infection alone or in addition to antibody testing. Direct detection may be more accurate than the Lyme disease two–tiered antibody testing standard that may result in false positives or negatives due to delayed antibody response or limited test sensitivity. Terminology Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as by producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Lyme disease (LD): An inflammatory disease caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, spread by ticks. Western blot: A laboratory procedure that uses gel electrophoresis followed by membrane transfer; an electrical field is applied across a gel containing the specimen, which causes the protein fractions to migrate apart; the protein fractions are then transferred to a membrane in a process called blotting. short_description: Pediatrics (congenital epigenetic disorders), whole genome methylation analysis by microarray for 50 or more genes, blood

lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Using a blood specimen from a patient following a kidney transplant, the test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) of specific parts of the transcriptome (mRNA transcribed from DNA) to evaluate gene expression related to immune response. The test uses an algorithmic analysis of the findings to report a risk score for acute or subclinical graft rejection. Explanation Using a blood specimen from a patient following a kidney transplant, the lab analyst uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) of specific parts of the transcriptome (messenger RNA transcribed from DNA) to evaluate gene expression related to immune response and other biologically important process involved in transplant rejection. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results as raw data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. The Tuteva™ algorithm results in a risk score for acute or subclinical graft rejection. Clinicians may order this test as part of kidney transplant follow–up testing, possibly performing the test sequentially over time depending on the findings. The risk–of–rejection score, coupled with clinical and pathological findings, may help the clinician balance protocols for immunosuppression and also detect early signs of graft (transplanted tissue) injury or rejection. Transcriptome: The collection of messenger RNA (mRNA) expressed by an organism, or by a particular type of cell or tissue. Transplant: (Noun) Tissue or organs removed from one person (donor) and placed in another (recipient), also transplantation, allotransplantation; tissue moved from within one location in the body to another, also allograft, autotransplantation; (verb) to transfer aforementioned tissue or organs. Explanation The lab analyst uses liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) to evaluate a plasma specimen for 14 acyl carnitines (a kind of organic compound) and products of metabolism related to microbes in the body (microbiome). LC–MS/MS is an automated laboratory platform that separates, identifies, and quantifies the level of specific chemical compounds in a specimen. This procedure is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA) test, which means that it includes both the analytical services to produce test results, and algorithmic analysis of those results (and possibly other patient data) to report a risk or prognostic score. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS): An automated laboratory test that combines liquid chromatography (LC), which separates components by passing the mixture through a mobile phase in which the components move at different rates, and two mass spectrometry (MS) steps, first to identify components by mass–to–charge ratio, and then to quantify the amounts of the components. Microbiome: Set of microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi, that live in a specific environment such as the human gut or skin. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. The analysis generates millions of DNA and RNA reads (sequences of base pairs) from the specimen. short_description: Targeted genomic sequence analysis panel, solid organ neoplasm, cell-free circulating DNA analysis of 83 or more genes, interrogation for sequence variants, gene copy number amplifications, gene rearrangements, microsatellite instability and tumor mutational burden

Microsatellite instability: The tendency of genes to mutate due to impaired DNA mismatch repair (MMR). Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Neoplasm: An abnormal mass or other tissue growth that can be benign or cancerous. The test uses a rapid automated platform to analyze single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that indicate chromosome copy number for chromosomes 13, 18, and 21. The platform uses an algorithmic analysis to report a risk score for each trisomy (13, 18, and 21), and includes a report of fetal sex, if requested. The test screens for 120 or more drugs and metabolites (breakdown products) in a urine specimen using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). The evaluation includes an algorithmic analysis of the drugs and metabolites identified to report the presence or absence of risk for a significant adverse drug event (ADE). short_description: Oncology (neoplasia), exome and transcriptome sequence analysis for sequence variants, gene copy number amplifications and deletions, gene rearrangements, microsatellite instability and tumor mutational burden utilizing DNA and RNA from tumor with DNA from normal blood or saliva for subtraction, report of clinically significant mutation(s) with therapy associations
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0329U only for Oncomap™ ExTra from Genomic Health Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of Exact Sciences Inc. The test evaluates tumor tissue using next–generation sequencing (NGS) for DNA sequencing of all genes associated with solid tumor mutations (whole exome) and expression of RNA (whole transcriptome). The procedure also sequences DNA from blood or saliva to rule out any mutations not associated with the tumor. Explanation Processing a tumor tissue specimen and a normal specimen (blood or saliva) from the patient using a next–generation sequencing (NGS) platform, the lab analyst sequences all protein–producing genes (exome) and a targeted group of other DNA regions relevant to cancer. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. The test evaluates copy number variants (CNVs), gene rearrangements, and the extent of mutation (microsatellite instability, which is the disposition to mutation; and tumor mutational burden, which is an estimate of the level of mutation). The test also evaluates RNA [removed]transcriptome) for changes relevant to cancer. The resulting report focuses on clinically significant genetic changes that occur in the tumor but not the normal specimen, along with a list of therapies associated with the findings. Especially in cases of rare, aggressive, or difficult–to–treat cancers, clinicians may use this test to identify specific mutations in the cancer genes (genomic profile) and link those changes to available therapeutic treatments. The recommended treatments may span chemotherapeutic agents, immunotherapy, and other targeted therapies. Explanation The lab analyst performs optical genomic mapping (OGM) using the Saphyr® System from Bionano Genomics Inc., which allows optical evaluation of the patient’s chromosomes for large scale changes in DNA, such as structural variants (SVs) and copy number variants (CNVs). The single assay provides findings similar to what would otherwise require a combination of cytogenetic techniques such as karyotyping, chromosomal microarrays (CMAs), and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Clinicians may order this test to detect all relevant chromosomal aberrations that impact diagnosis and treatment of hematologic neoplasms such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), multiple myeloma (MM), plasma cell myeloma (PCM), chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), and more. Cytogenetics: Genetic studies related to structural variation of chromosomes. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH): A laboratory test in which a special stain that includes a DNA or RNA probe, which selectively attaches to a target segment of DNA or RNA, is applied to a tissue sample in situ hybridization (ISH); the probe includes some kind of marker, often a fluorescent molecule, which can be analyzed with a fluorescence microscope to detect and localize the target in the tissue (fluorescence ISH, or FISH); fluorescence describes a substance which absorbs and emits light. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. short_description: Oncology (pan-tumor), genetic profiling of 8 DNA-regulatory (epigenetic) markers by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), whole blood, reported as a high or low probability of responding to immune checkpoint-inhibitor therapy
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0332U only for EpiSwitch® CiRT (Checkpoint–inhibitor Response Test) from Next Bio–Research Services LLC and Oxford BioDynamics PLC. Using a whole blood specimen from a cancer patient, the test identifies and quantifies eight biomarkers of non–gene (epigenetic) factors that could impact patient response to specific cancer drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors. Explanation Using a whole blood specimen from a cancer patient, the lab analyst performs quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) to analyze eight biomarkers of non–gene (epigenetic) factors that can influence how genes are expressed. The test specifically evaluates chromosome conformation signatures (CCSs), which impact gene activity based on the way that chromosomal DNA is packaged. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. This test evaluates epigenetic factors and reports the findings as a probability score of high or low likelihood that the patient would respond to immune checkpoint–inhibitor therapy. Clinicians may order this test for patients with any type of cancer that might be responsive to immune checkpoint–inhibitor therapy. Checkpoint proteins slow the immune response, and some cancers produce the proteins, allowing the cancer to grow unchecked. Certain drugs act as immunotherapy to inhibit the checkpoint proteins, thus enabling the body’s own immune response to attack cancer cells. The 0032U test provides clinicians with a probability score indicating the patient’s likely response to immune checkpoint–inhibitor drugs such as atezolizumab (Tecentriq®), ipilimumab (Yervoy®), nivolumab (Opdivo®), and pembrolizumab (Keytruda®). Checkpoint proteins: Proteins made by immune cells such as T cells that slow the immune response to keep it from getting too strong (in check); some cancer cells also produce checkpoint proteins, thus keeping the body from attacking the cancer. Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Epigenetic: Nongenetic factors that influence how genes are expressed (either activated or suppressed). Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Immunotherapy: Treatment of a disease by suppressing or otherwise manipulating the immunity of the body. Report 0333U only for HelioLiver™ Test from Fulgent Genetics LLC and Helio Health Inc. Using a whole blood specimen, the test evaluates cell–free DNA (cfDNA) and protein tumor markers to help detect early liver cancer in patients at high risk for developing the disease. Explanation Using a whole blood specimen from a patient at high risk for developing liver cancer, the lab analyst evaluates the specimen for liver cancer markers. The test measures levels of two protein biomarkers: alpha–fetoprotein (AFP/AFP–L3) and the oncoprotein des–gammacarboxy–prothrombin (DCP). The test also extracts circulating cell–free DNA (cfDNA) from the blood specimen and evaluates patterns of methylation (which represses gene expression) specific to hepatocellular carcinoma. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Clinicians may order this test for patients over 21 with a liver cirrhosis diagnosis who are at high risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). The blood test is a “liquid biopsy” that allows early detection of possible liver cancer. The test algorithm provides a result of “normal” or “abnormal.” If the test result is normal, the clinician may repeat the test every three to six months for surveillance. If the test result is abnormal, the clinician may proceed with diagnostic imaging. Cirrhosis: A chronic disease of the liver with inflammation and fibrous changes, frequently caused by hepatitis or alcoholism. Using a blood or saliva sample, the test is a whole genome sequence analysis to identify genetic variants that may be related to clinical fetal or pregnancy symptoms, or variants that could indicate rare heritable disorders that the parent may have passed on to the fetus. Explanation The lab analyst evaluates a blood or saliva specimen from a parent of the proband fetus using next–generation sequencing (NGS) of the whole genome and mitochondrial DNA for variants related to rare heritable (constitutional) disorders. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. The 0336U test evaluates the parental genome for copy number variants such as insertions, deletions, and duplications, plus inversions and short tandem repeat (STR) gene expansions. The test also evaluates for aneuploidy, which is an abnormal chromosome number, and uniparental disomy (UPD), which occurs when the fertilized egg includes two copies or a partial copy of a chromosome from one parent and none from the other parent. Clinicians may order this test for one or both parents when abnormal ultrasound findings indicate that amniocentesis is medically necessary, and the fetal genome analysis identifies variants of concern. In that case, the fetus is the proband patient, which is the first member in a family to receive genetic testing, and each parent would be a comparator patient. Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Genome: The entire genetic material of an organism, which means the entire DNA sequence. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. These analyses may include a range of medical laboratory tests including, but not limited to, multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP). The descriptor nomenclature follows, where possible, existing code conventions (eg, MAAA, GSP). Unless specifically noted, even though the Proprietary Laboratory Analyses section of the code set is located at the end of the Pathology and Laboratory section of the code set, a PLA code does not fulfill Category I code criteria. PLA codes are not required to fulfill the Category I criteria. The standards for inclusion in the PLA section are: The test must be commercially available in the United States for use on human specimens and The clinical laboratory or manufacturer that offers the test must request the code. For similar laboratory analyses that fulfill Category I criteria, see codes listed in the numeric 80000 series. When a PLA code is available to report a given proprietary laboratory service, that PLA code takes precedence. The service should not be reported with any other CPT® code(s) and other CPT® code(s) should not be used to report services that may be reported with that specific PLA code. These codes encompass all analytical services required for the analysis (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization and detection). For molecular analyses, additional procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection [codes 88380 and 88381]) may be reported separately. Codes in this subsection are released on a quarterly basis to expedite dissemination for reporting. PLA codes will be published electronically on the AMA CPT® website (ama-assn.org/cpt-pla-codes), distributed via CPT® data files on a quarterly basis, and, at a minimum, made available in print annually in the CPT® codebook. See the Introduction section of the CPT® code set for a complete list of the dates of release and implementation. All codes that are included in this section are also included in Appendix O, with the procedure's proprietary name. In order to report a PLA code, the analysis performed must fulfill the code descriptor and must be the test represented by the proprietary name listed in Appendix O. When more than one PLA has an identical descriptor, the codes will be denoted by the symbol "â™“." All PLA tests will have assigned codes in the PLA section of the code set. short_description: Oncology (prostate), mRNA expression profiling of HOXC6 and DLX1, reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), first-void urine following digital rectal examination, algorithm reported as probability of high-grade cancer
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0339U for SelectMDx® for Prostate Cancer from MDxHealth® Inc. Using a urine specimen, the test evaluates the activity (gene expression) of two genes: HOXC6 and DLX1. An algorithmic analysis of the findings reports a probability score for the likelihood that the patient has high–grade prostate cancer. Explanation The lab analyst performs the test using a first–void urine specimen following digital rectal examination (DRE) to evaluate the activity (gene expression) of two genes: HOXC6 and DLX1. The procedure involves reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR), which uses RNA in the specimen as a template to make DNA (reverse transcription) and creates more copies of the DNA using PCR. The RT–PCR process creates a gene expression profile, indicating which DNA sequences are actively expressed — that is, transcribed to RNA and translated to a protein that performs some function in the body. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Using the urine HOXC6 and DLX1 mRNA biomarker levels plus patient data such as age, prostate specific antigen (PSA) level, DRE findings, and family history of prostate cancer, the algorithm provides a probability score for the likelihood that the patient has high–grade prostate cancer. Clinicians may order this test for patients with elevated PSA test results to evaluate the patient’s risk of having high–grade prostate cancer. The clinician may use the test results to help determine whether prostate biopsy is indicated. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation).?? Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Prostate specific antigen (PSA): An enzyme produced in the prostate gland that when elevated indicates the presence of prostate cancer. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR): A technique to measure specimen RNA levels by reacting RNA with the enzyme reverse transcriptase to produce complementary DNA (cDNA), which is more stable than RNA, and then create more copies of the DNA by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Tips Use this code only for the appropriate proprietary test; report one unit of this code for a single specimen analyzed on a single date of service. Distinguish this test from the similar test reported using 0011M. Additional Info “U” codes are included in the CPT® code set to identify specific proprietary laboratory analyses (PLA) tests. PLA codes take precedence over the usual 80000 series codes for laboratory/pathology. Use this code only for the above–described test; do not report this test using any other CPT® code. PLA code descriptors follow existing code conventions when possible, and lab techniques used include multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP), among others. short_description: Oncology (pan-cancer), analysis of minimal residual disease (MRD) from plasma, with assays personalized to each patient based on prior next-generation sequencing of the patient's tumor and germline DNA, reported as absence or presence of MRD, with disease-burden correlation, if appropriate
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0340U only for Signatera™ from Natera Inc. The test uses a cancer patient’s plasma specimen for a targeted sequence analysis using circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). The targeted DNA is based on a prior next–generation sequence (NGS) analysis of the patient’s tumor and germline (inherited) DNA for a customized evaluation of minimal residual disease (MRD). Explanation The lab analyst processes a cancer patient’s plasma specimen to preserve cell–free DNA (cfDNA), then isolate and extract circulating–tumor DNA (ct–DNA). The analyst evaluates the ct–DNA using a next–generation sequencing (NGS) targeted gene panel. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. This test compares ct–DNA to a customized DNA panel based on a prior next–generation sequence (NGS) analysis of the patient’s tumor and germline (inherited) DNA. Clinicians may order this test at several points during a patient’s treatment for many forms of cancer. Because the test evaluates a customized DNA profile specific to the patient’s cancer, evaluating ct–DNA can help indicate the patient’s minimal residual disease (MRD) following treatment. Clinicians may use the test to detect MRD after surgery, to monitor cancer recurrence after adjuvant therapy, or to monitor treatment response after relapse. Terminology Adjuvant therapy: Treatment provided in addition to primary therapy; in cases of cancer, adjuvant therapy usually refers to chemotherapy or radiotherapy or both following surgery to remove the cancer. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Cell–free DNA (cfDNA): Nonencapsulated DNA in the form of nucleic acid fragments that enter the bloodstream during apoptosis (programmed, or normal, cell death) or necrosis (cell death due to loss of blood supply from injury, radiation, or chemicals). Circulating–tumor DNA (ctDNA): DNA that comes from a tumor and circulates in the blood; a specific type of cell–free DNA. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Germline: Genes that occurs in every cell of an organism, having been inherited from egg and sperm of parents; germline (constitutional) mutations can be passed from parent to progeny. Minimal residual disease (MRD): Low level of cancer cells remaining in the body following cancer treatment. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. PLA code descriptors follow existing code conventions when possible, and lab techniques used include multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) and genomic sequencing procedures (GSP), among others.
