short_description: Fetal aneuploidy DNA sequencing comparative analysis, fetal DNA from products of conception, reported as normal (euploidy), monosomy, trisomy, or partial deletion/duplication, mosaicism, and segmental aneuploid
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0341U only for Single Cell Prenatal Diagnosis (SCPD) Test from Luna Genetics Inc. The test uses a maternal blood sample early in pregnancy to isolate fetal cells for DNA sequencing. The assay evaluates fetal cells for various aneuploidies (abnormal chromosome number), duplication/deletion variants, and mosaicism (cells with different genotypes). Explanation Using a maternal blood specimen taken between eight and 22 weeks gestation, the lab analyst isolates fetal cells for individual DNA analysis. The test evaluates for aneuploidies such as Down syndrome, trisomy 13, trisomy 18, and other chromosomal abnormalities. The test can also detect gene deletions/duplications larger than 1.5 million bases (Mb) and 2 Mb, respectively, which represents most mutations related to disease. By evaluating distinct cells, the test may detect mosaicism (cells with different genotypes), if present. Clinicians may order this test instead of more common tests such as cell–free noninvasive prenatal testing (cfNIPT) for earlier detection, fewer false positives due to maternal genotype, and higher resolution. In most cases, the test may preclude the need for more invasive testing that presents risk to the fetus, such as amniocentesis and chorionic villi sampling (CVS). Terminology Amniocentesis: A procedure in which a small sample of amniotic fluid is drawn out of the uterus through a needle inserted in the abdomen. Aneuploidy: Chromosome mutation involving an abnormal chromosome number, such as one or three chromosome copies in the nucleus of cells that have a normally have two chromosomes. Chorionic villi sampling: A prenatal test in which a sample of chorionic villi (tiny, fingerlike growths found in the placenta and made up of fetal cells) is removed from the placenta to diagnose congenital abnormalities. Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Fetal aneuploidy: Fetal chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome, Edwards syndrome or Patau syndrome. Genotype: The genetic, internally coded information of a particular organism or person, distinct from the expressed features or the phenotype. Mosaicism: Genetic condition when an individual has more than one genotype in different sets of cells. short_description: Oncology (pancreatic cancer), multiplex immunoassay of C5, C4, cystatin C, factor B, osteoprotegerin (OPG), gelsolin, IGFBP3, CA125 and multiplex electrochemiluminescent immunoassay (ECLIA) for CA19-9, serum, diagnostic algorithm reported qualitatively as positive, negative, or borderline
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0342U only for IMMray® PanCan–d from Immunovia Inc. The test evaluates a serum specimen using two different immunoassays (biochemical tests) for the nine biomarkers listed in the code. The procedure includes an algorithm using the test results and other patient data to report the findings as positive, negative, or borderline for pancreatic cancer. Explanation The lab analyst processes the serum sample and applies it to a microarray slide with fluorescently tagged antibodies for tumor and immunoregulatory biomarkers listed in the code. A fluorescence scanner measures the level of each biomarker except CA19–9. The analyst separately measures CA19–9 level in the serum using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA). This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Using the biochemical test results plus patient data such as age, the algorithmic analysis provides one of three findings: high–risk signature present, negative for high–risk signature, or borderline. Clinicians may order this test as an early indicator of pancreatic cancer for patients at risk of developing the disease due to family history or known genetic mutation. The test is not appropriate for screening the general population. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA): A laboratory testing method that uses the electrochemical properties of specific markers to produce light and identify a substance with a luminometer. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Microarray: A lab device composed of a surface with a grid of dots containing different DNA sequences that act as probes to capture targets in the specimen; used to map gene expression; sometimes called a gene chip. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Pancreatic cancer: Cancer that begins in the cells of the pancreas that produce the enzymes that break down food and the hormones that help control blood sugar; it is often found late, spreads quickly, is difficult to treat, and is often fatal. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Explanation The lab analyst evaluates a whole blood or buccal (cheek) swab specimen using next–generation sequencing (NGS) to evaluate 27 target genes for specific variants related to drug metabolism and function. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. The test also includes a pharmacogenomic analysis comparing the genetic results to a database of biomarkers for specific drugs. The test report lists specific drugs, indicating whether the patient’s genotype indicates an expected gene–drug interaction ranging from “limited” to “major” that could impact the drug performance, dosing, and clinical utility. Clinicians may use this test for patients undergoing treatment for a variety of medical conditions to help evaluate specific gene–drug interactions and guide clinical decision making regarding choice and dosing of specific drugs. Terminology Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Genotype: The genetic, internally coded information of a particular organism or person, distinct from the expressed features or the phenotype. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Pharmacogenomics: The study of how a person’s genotype and phenotype affect their response to drugs. Phenotype: The observable traits of an organism due to interaction of genes and the environment; distinct from the internally coded information of the genotype. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. The test uses a blood or saliva specimen for a targeted DNA sequence analysis for G1 and G2 variants in the APOL1 gene. The variant analysis aids in risk evaluation for kidney transplant donors and recipients. Explanation The lab analyst processes a blood or saliva specimen to extract DNA, then increases the number of copies of (amplifies) the Apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) gene using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Findings of both G1 and G2 variants increases the risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) by 41 percent above the risk for individuals with one or neither variant. Clinicians may order this test to aid in evaluation of potential kidney transplant donors of African descent. Explanation The lab analyst extracts cell–free DNA from an oropharyngeal or anal specimen from a patient with human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated cancer. An automated droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) platform fragments DNA into droplets, amplifies (increases the number) of DNA molecules using polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and quantifies the presence of 17 DNA biomarkers for HPV that is integrated into cancer cells (as opposed to nontumor derived HPV). This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Using the test data for 17 DNA fragments shed by cancer cells into the blood and other clinical data, the 0356U test includes an algorithmic analysis to report the likelihood of cancer recurrence. Clinicians may order this test for patients who have undergone treatment for HPV–associated cancer. Negative findings indicate the patient is cancer free, while quantified findings of tumor–associated HPV DNA circulating in the blood may indicate cancer recurrence. Clinicians may use the test findings alone or with more traditional follow–up imaging testing such as computed tomography (CT) scans. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps using chemiluminescence immunoassay (also called immunochemiluminometric assay, or IMAC) to measure the level of β–Amyloid peptides (protein fractions) 1–42 and 1–41 in a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen. The method involves using specific antibodies in test wells to bind with target peptides in the specimen. Following a wash step, the lab analyst labels each β–Amyloid antigen/antibody complex with a chemical that initiates light signals read by an instrument, which corresponds to the quantity of 1–42 and 1–41 β–Amyloid in the specimen. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. The algorithm for the 0358U test identifies the 1–42/1–40 ratio test findings as positive, likely positive, or negative for Alzheimer’s disease. Clinicians may order this test for patients aged 55 and older who are undergoing evaluation for symptoms of mild cognitive impairment. Prior to use of this test, clinicians relied on other methods that were more subjective such as cognitive assessment and possibly positron emission tomography (PET) brain imaging. short_description: Oncology (papillary thyroid cancer), gene-expression profiling via targeted hybrid capture-enrichment RNA sequencing of 82 content genes and 10 housekeeping genes, fine needle aspirate or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue, algorithm reported as one of three molecular subtypes
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0362U only for Thyroid GuidePx® from Protean BioDiagnostics. The test evaluates a formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue specimen from a patient with papillary thyroid cancer for expression of 82 genes and uses an algorithmic analysis to classify the molecular subtype as it relates to risk of recurrence. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical lab test on a fine needle aspirate or formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue from a papillary thyroid tumor by extracting nucleic acids, by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, and stabilizing and increasing the quantity of 82 target (content) RNA nucleic acid markers and 10 housekeeping (control) markers for next–generation sequencing (NGS) analysis. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. The 0362U test uses the genomic classification from the NGS results of the patient’s thyroid tumor plus clinical information, and the algorithmic analysis identifies the tumor as one of three subtypes that reflects the risk of cancer recurrence. Clinicians may order this test following thyroid surgery to inform treatment decisions for patients with papillary thyroid cancer, which can have a high rate of recurrence. The three molecular subtypes identified by the 0362U test stratify the tumor into three groups with decreasing risk of recurrence, which can guide clinicians in determining the best treatment alternatives. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Fine needle aspiration (FNA): A technique to obtain fluid, tissue, and/or cell samples for laboratory analysis by sucking (aspirating) them up into a syringe attached to a needle of very fine diameter inserted into the target area. Formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE): A method to preserve a tissue specimen, such as a biopsy, and prepare it for microscopic examination; the process uses formalin (formaldehyde) to preserve (fix) the tissue and paraffin to embed the tissue in a waxy block that can be sliced thin for viewing on a microscope slide. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance; also, in vascular surgery, instilling a clot–dissolving drug to break up a clot. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Papillary tumors: Fingerlike tumors that arise on a stem from the lining of an organ. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. Thyroid: A butterfly–shaped gland in the neck that secretes hormones regulating growth and development; the alae (singular ala) refer to the "wings" of the thyroid. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Subsequent, separately reportable tests repeat the procedure, but compare the findings to the original test to generate the MRD Tracking Report, which indicates whether the patient has remaining cells of the clonal cancer, called minimal residual disease (MRD). Clinicians may order this test for patients with several hematolymphoid cancers, such as B–cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), multiple myeloma (MM), or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). The clinician will order repeat tests, with the initial test identifying the specific mutations associated with the patient’s cancer (clonal identification). Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Minimal residual disease (MRD): Low level of cancer cells remaining in the body following cancer treatment. Neoplasm: An abnormal mass or other tissue growth that can be benign or cancerous. The report specifically identifies 23 variables describing lipid particle size and number that may more accurately predict adverse cardiovascular events. Explanation The lab analyst processes a serum or plasma specimen using 2–D diffusion–ordered nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Diffusion–ordered spectroscopy (DOSY) separates NMR signals using pulse field gradients and measuring spin echo spectra and signal decay to determine lipoprotein particle size and number. short_description: Targeted genomic sequence analysis panel, solid organ neoplasm, DNA (523 genes) and RNA (55 genes) by next-generation sequencing, interrogation for sequence variants, gene copy number amplifications, gene rearrangements, microsatellite instability, and tumor mutational burden
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0379U only for Solid Tumor Expanded Panel from Quest Diagnostics. The test uses a next–generation sequencing (NGS) targeted sequence analysis panel for a tumor specimen to evaluate DNA for 523 genes and RNA for 55 genes. The results may aid with diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment selection for patients with solid tumors. Explanation The lab analyst evaluates a patient specimen, such as tumor tissue or cells, using a next–generation sequencing (NGS) targeted gene panel. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. This test performs NGS of 522 genes from DNA and 55 genes from RNA, compares the digital sequence library from the specimen to a reference genome, and classifies variants. The comparison panel focuses on specifically selected genomic changes associated with actionable variants that can influence clinical decisions related to diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. The test detects single nucleotide variants (SNVs), copy number variations (CNVs), and the extent of mutation through microsatellite instability (MSI), which is the predisposition to mutation, and tumor mutational burden (TMB), which is an estimate of the level of mutation. Clinicians may order this test to aid with diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment selection for patients with solid tumors. Terminology Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Genome: The entire genetic material of an organism, which means the entire DNA sequence. Microsatellite instability: The tendency of genes to mutate due to impaired DNA mismatch repair (MMR). Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Nucleotides: Biochemicals — sometimes called “bases” — that form the building blocks of nucleic acids, DNA and RNA; DNA is made up of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T), while RNA uses uracil (U) in place of T; each base will pair with only one specific “complementary” base when forming DNA or RNA strands. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. Targeted region sequencing: A variation on targeted gene sequencing that focuses on single–nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), insertions/deletions (InDels), copy number variations (CNVs), and structural variants (SVs) which enables detection of rare variants with higher sensitivity and specificity. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. The test evaluates a patient–collected blood spot specimen for levels of allo–isoleucine, leucine, isoleucine, and valine using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). Clinicians may order this test for patients diagnosed with maple sugar urine disease (MSUD) to help monitor their treatment. MSUD is an inborn error of metabolism caused by a genetic mutation that interferes with the body’s ability to metabolize branched–chain amino acids (isoleucine, leucine, and valine) present in food, allowing them to build up to toxic levels. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0385U only for PromarkerD from Sonic Reference Laboratory, Proteomics International Pty Ltd. Using enzyme–linked immunoassay (ELISA) method, the test evaluates a blood (plasma) sample for biomarkers of kidney disease associated with diabetes. The test combines these results with the patient’s age, HDL–cholesterol level, and estimated glomerular filtration rate to report a risk score for developing kidney disease. Explanation Using a plasma specimen, the lab analyst performs the technical steps for enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to measure the levels of three biomarkers related to developing kidney disease: apolipoprotein A4 (ApoA4), CD5 antigen–like (CD5L), and insulin–like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGFBP3). The method involves autoantibodies in the specimen binding to a “capture” antigen and an enzyme labeled “detection” antigen that creates a chromogenic (color) reaction to quantify the level of each autoantibody in the specimen. An autoantibody is an antibody the immune system makes that targets substances formed by a person’s own body. This test includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. The 0385U test combines the ELISA results with the patient’s age, HDL–cholesterol level, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to report a risk score for developing kidney disease. GFR is the rate at which the kidneys can process the elements in the blood so they can be eliminated through urine. Clinicians may order this test for patients diagnosed with diabetes to help assess their risk level for developing diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as by producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Enzyme: A biological compound that acts as a selective catalyst to increase the rate and specificity of certain biochemical reactions, such as breaking down a specific compound. Enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA): A laboratory testing method using an enzyme attached to an antigen or antibody used as a marker to detect a specific substance, such as another antigen or antibody. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR): The rate at which the kidneys can process the elements in the blood so they can be eliminated through urine. High–density lipoprotein (HDL): A constituent or fraction of total cholesterol that transfers cholesterol from body tissues to the liver, essential and good for the body. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. short_description: Oncology (melanoma), autophagy and beclin 1 regulator 1 (AMBRA1) and loricrin (AMLo) by immunohistochemistry, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue, report for risk of progression Notes: (Do not report 0387U in conjunction with 88341, 88342)
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0387U describes AMBLor® melanoma prognostic test from Avero® Diagnostics. The test uses immunohistochemistry staining on a formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) melanoma tissue specimen to identify two biomarkers. Using an algorithmic analysis of the biomarker levels, the test reports a risk score for melanoma progression and metastasis. Explanation The test evaluates immunohistochemistry stains for two biomarkers, autophagy and beclin 1 regulator 1 (AMBRA1) and loricrin (AMLo), on formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded tissue from a patient with early–stage melanoma (stage I or II based on American Joint Committee on Cancer [AJCC] staging criteria). The procedure compares levels of AMBRA1 and loricrin in skin overlying the tumor compared to clear skin margins. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. If immunohistochemistry indicates normal expression of either or both biomarkers in skin overlying the tumor, the algorithm predicts low risk of progression to metastasis. Clinicians may order this test to identify whether a patient with early–stage melanoma is at low risk of disease progression. The results may allow the clinician to personalize a follow–up schedule. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE): A method to preserve a tissue specimen, such as a biopsy, and prepare it for microscopic examination; the process uses formalin (formaldehyde) to preserve (fix) the tissue and paraffin to embed the tissue in a waxy block that can be sliced thin for viewing on a microscope slide. Immunohistochemistry: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood; also called immunoassay. Melanoma: A deadly form of cancer, primarily of the skin, but it can affect other organs that contain melanocytes, cells that produce the pigment melanin. Metastasis: Cancer that has spread from its original location to another place in the body; also known as metastatic cancer. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. The test evaluates a patient blood specimen for RNA expression of two genes listed in the code and reports a risk score for Kawasaki disease (KD), a fever of unknown origin in children. Explanation The lab analyst evaluates a blood specimen for activity (gene expression) of two genes: alphainducible protein 27 (IFI27) and mast cell–expressed membrane protein 1 (MCEMP1). The procedure involves reverse transcription–quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT–qPCR), which uses RNA in the specimen as a template to make DNA (reverse transcription) and creates more copies of the DNA using PCR. The RT–qPCR process creates a gene expression profile indicating which DNA sequences are actively expressed — that is, transcribed to RNA and translated to a protein that performs some function in the body. Using the blood RNA expression levels plus patient data such as age and possibly clinical factors, the algorithm provides a probability score for the likelihood that the patient has Kawasaki disease (KD), also known as Kawasaki syndrome. Clinicians may order this test for infants and children with fever lasting more than five days presenting with at least four other symptoms such as inflammation of the eye conjunctiva, reddening of lips and oral cavity, skin rash, reddening of palms and soles, and enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck. Results of the test can aid in early diagnosis of KD in children, resulting in earlier clinical intervention. Left untreated, KD may result in coronary artery lesions that can lead to aneurysm and may adversely impact other organs. short_description: Drug metabolism (depression, anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder [ADHD]), gene-drug interactions, variant analysis of 16 genes, including deletion/duplication analysis of CYP2D6, reported as impact of gene-drug interaction for each drug
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0392U only for Medication Management Neuropsychiatric Panel from RCA Laboratory Services LLC d/b/a GENETWORx. The test uses a buccal (cheek) swab specimen for a targeted sequence analysis of 16 genes as well as CYP2D6 duplication/deletion analysis and reports the impact of gene–drug interaction for each psychiatric drug based on the patient’s genetics and other relevant factors. Explanation The lab analyst processes a buccal (cheek) swab specimen using an automated platform to extract nucleic acids and perform real–time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) to evaluate 16 genes and CYP2D6 duplication/deletion mutations that could impact gene–drug interactions for psychiatric drugs. Using the sequence analysis results plus patient data, such as lifestyle factors and medication history, the findings are compared to medication guidelines, such as FDA Black Box Warnings and published clinical trial results, to provide a medication action plan (MAP) for possible gene–drug interactions for each of nearly 30 psychiatric drugs. Clinicians may order this test for patients with psychiatric conditions, such as depression, anxiety, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), to help evaluate the expected patient response to each psychiatric medication in terms of efficacy and dosage. This is a pharmacogenomics (PGX) test, which helps clinicians evaluate how a person’s genetics and other factors can interact with a patient’s response to drugs. Metabolism of many commonly prescribed medications, such as Prozac®, Paxil™, Zoloft®, Effexor®, and Haldol®, are impacted by mutations that duplicate or delete nucleic acid sequences in the CYP2D6 gene, impacting the dosage and efficacy of the drugs. Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction, called PCR, or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Pharmacogenomics: The study of how a person’s genotype and phenotype affect their response to drugs. Targeted (gene) sequencing: Molecular gene sequencing technology, often next–generation sequencing (NGS), that focuses on a specific gene, set of genes, or gene region for analysis, useful in identifying whether genes or genetic mutations known to be associated with specific conditions are present; in NGS, multiple genes can be assessed across many samples in parallel at the same time. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Neurology (eg, Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), detection of misfolded α-synuclein protein by seed amplification assay, qualitative
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code describes only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Code 0393U describes SYNTap® Biomarker Test from Amprion Clinical Laboratory. The test detects misfolded α–synuclein proteins present in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen and serves as a biomarker for certain neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Lewy body dementia (LBD). Explanation Using a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen, the lab analyst performs a seed amplification assay using Amprion’s proprietary method. The procedure involves adding fluorescently labeled normal (not misfolded) α–synuclein (α–syn) protein to the sample, then identifying any misfolded α–syn protein aggregates present in the CSF specimen. If misfolded α–syn protein aggregates are present, they “seed” the labeled normal protein, meaning the misfolded protein aggregates cause the normal proteins to misfold and aggregate. If the CSF specimen contains no misfolded proteins, the fluorescence is undetectable, and the test is negative. If fluorescence indicates the presence of misfolded protein aggregates, the test is positive, serving as a biomarker for Parkinson’s disease (PD), Lewy body dementia (LBD), and possibly other conditions that may involve misfolded α–syn protein, such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). Clinicians may order this test for symptomatic patients to aid in early diagnosis of PD or LBD. Terminology Alzheimer’s disease: A slowly progressive form of dementia characterized by beta–amyloid plaques (microscopic clumps of pieces of protein), tangles (strands) of the tau protein (abundant in the central nervous system but not elsewhere), brain inflammation, and damage and eventual death of brain cells. Biomarker, biological marker, biochemical marker: A measurable substance, such as an enzyme, protein, or gene, that is an indicator of a condition, disease, or normal or abnormal process. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): A clear serum–like fluid that circulates in the ventricles of the brain and around the surface of the brain and spinal cord; it helps maintain uniform pressure within the spinal cord and brain. Lewy body dementia: A progressive neurologic disease characterized by protein deposits (Lewy bodies) in the brain causing mental decline and possible hallucinations, as well as loss of motor control Parkinson’s disease: A progressive disease of the nervous system with characteristic features of tremors, rigidity, and slowness of movements, also known as parkinsonism. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. The test identifies the level of 16 perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) compounds present in the serum or plasma specimen using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). Explanation The lab analyst uses liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) to evaluate a plasma or serum specimen for 16 perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) compounds such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS). This is a quantitative test that measures the level of any of the 16 substances detected. Clinicians may order this test for patients known to have high exposure to PFAS compounds, such as workers involved in manufacturing using the substances or people drinking water found to be contaminated with high levels of PFAS. Although not linked to specific health conditions, PFAS may lead to increased cholesterol levels, increased risk of high blood pressure or preeclampsia in pregnant women, changes in liver enzymes, decreased vaccine response in children, and increased risk of kidney or testicular cancer. Terminology Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS): An automated laboratory test that combines liquid chromatography (LC), which separates components by passing the mixture through a mobile phase in which the components move at different rates, and mass spectrometry (MS), a technique to identify the components and then amounts of a mixture by ionizing, separating by mass–to–charge ratio, and detecting the components; tandem refers to the two steps, first to detect or identify the components and second to quantify the amounts of the components. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. Quantitative measurement: Test to measure the specific quantity of a substance in the specimen. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0395U only for OncobiotaLUNG from Micronoma™. The test uses a plasma specimen from a patient with an indeterminate lung nodule to extract and evaluate microbial DNA and two proteins listed in the code for an algorithmic analysis to predict the patient as high or low risk for malignancy. Explanation The lab analyst processes a plasma sample from a patient who has been diagnosed with an indeterminate lung nodule to extract and evaluate microbial DNA using next–generation sequencing (NGS). Microorganisms in the body (microbiome) may serve as biomarkers to detect early–stage cancer. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. The lab analyst also performs an immunoassay to detect levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and osteopontin (OPN) in the serum specimen, which may be biomarkers of malignant changes and metastasis. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Using the test results plus patient data such as age and smoking history, the algorithm provides a determination that the patient is at high or low risk of a malignant lung nodule. Clinicians may order this test for patients with an indeterminate lung nodule identified incidentally by a low–dose computed tomography (LDCT) scan for other conditions or identified during LDCT lung cancer screening for high risk patients ages 50 plus who have smoked a pack or more of cigarettes a day for 20 plus years. This is a noninvasive liquid biopsy that assigns a high or low risk score that the nodule is likely to be malignant. The results may reduce the need for risks associated with follow–up invasive testing, such as lung biopsy. Terminology Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA): A protein that is elevated in blood plasma in a variety of cancerous and benign conditions, such as gallbladder, colon, pancreatic, stomach, lung, and breast cancers, pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and alcoholic cirrhosis; CEA is also used to monitor cancer treatment response. Liquid biopsy: Blood test to find biomarkers or bits of nucleic acids or cancer cells that break off from a tumor and circulate in the blood; may be useful for finding early–stage cancer. Microbiome: Set of microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi, that live in a specific environment such as the human gut or skin. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. short_description: Gastroenterology (Barrett's esophagus), P16, RUNX3, HPP1, and FBN1 DNA methylation analysis using PCR, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue, algorithm reported as risk score for progression to high-grade dysplasia or cancer
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0398U for ESOPREDICT® Barrett’s Esophagus Risk Classifier Assay from Capsulomics Inc. d/b/a Previse. Using esophageal cells obtained from a formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) biopsy specimen, the test evaluates methylation status of the genes listed in the code. With an algorithmic analysis of those findings, the results are reported as a risk score for progression to high–grade dysplasia or esophageal cancer. Explanation Using formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue from an esophageal biopsy, the lab analyst extracts DNA and treats it with bisulfite. The lab method uses quantitative real–time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) to determine methylation levels in promotor regions of four genes (P16, RUNX3, HPP1, and FBN1), which can serve as a biomarker for cancer. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Using the methylation analysis plus patient data and possibly clinical factors, the algorithm provides a probability score for the likelihood that the patient’s Barrett esophagus (BE) will progress to high–grade dysplasia (abnormal growth or development) or esophageal carcinoma (EAC). The test reports the findings as a risk score of low/favorable, intermediate/unfavorable, or intermediate/high, and also provides a 5–year probability of progressing to EAC. Clinicians may order this test for patients with BE using a biopsy acquired during an endoscopy. The method involves antibodies in the specimen binding to a “capture” antigen and an enzyme–labeled “detection” antigen that creates a chromogenic (color) reaction to detect the target antibodies, if present. short_description: Obstetrics (expanded carrier screening), 145 genes by next-generation sequencing, fragment analysis and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification, DNA, reported as carrier positive or negative
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Using a blood or buccal (cheek) swab specimen from a prospective parent, the test evaluates 145 genes to identify variants that may indicate the person is a carrier of a mutation that could result in a rare inherited disorder that could be passed on to a child, such as cystic fibrosis. Explanation Using a blood or buccal (cheek) swab specimen from a prospective parent, the lab analyst extracts DNA and uses polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify (increase the number of) and evaluate 145 genes using next–generation sequencing (NGS). The genes are relevant to a broad range of genetic conditions that can be inherited. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. The analyst also evaluates the extracted DNA using multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification (MLPA), which is a test designed to detect large deletions and duplications of nucleotide sequences that normal DNA sequencing methods do not detect. The test produces a report identifying the person as positive or negative for a variant known to be relevant to a specific inherited condition. Clinicians may order this test for patients who are considering having children and are concerned about possibly passing on an inherited genetic condition. The test evaluates genes recommended by the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) and American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) for prenatal testing. By evaluating both parents, clinicians can help the couple understand the risk of having a child who inherits a condition such as cystic fibrosis, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, or Fragile X Syndrome. Cystic fibrosis: An inherited disorder characterized by the production of thick, sticky mucus that blocks pancreatic ducts and clogs the lungs. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Fragile X syndrome: A genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the FMR1 gene, resulting in intellectual disability and certain facial characteristics. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Muscular dystrophy: A group of genetic diseases in which progressive weakness and degeneration of the skeletal muscles that control movement occurs. Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. The test evaluates a vaginal, endocervical, or male urine specimen using a multiplex amplified probe technique to detect Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis, and Mycoplasma genitalium, which cause common sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Explanation The lab analyst processes the specimen, such as an endocervical swab specimen, vaginal swab specimen, gynecological specimen collected in ThinPrep® PreservCyt® solution, or male urine, using an Alinity m instrument. The automated system extracts DNA and uses reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR) to amplify (increase the number of) target genes to detect and differentiate Chlamydia trachomatis RNA, Neisseria gonorrhoeae DNA, Trichomonas vaginalis RNA, and Mycoplasma genitalium RNA. The procedure uses multiplex probe technique and reports the findings for each organism as “detected” or “not detected,” typically in under two hours. Clinicians may order this test for male or female patients exhibiting symptoms, such as pain, sores, odor, or discharge, of a sexually transmitted infection (STI). These STIs are often asymptomatic, however, so the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends annual screening for certain sexually active patients, with same day test and treat, if possible. Gonococcal infection: A venereal or sexually transmitted disease (STD) that results from infection with the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae, also referred to as gonorrhea. Mycoplasma genitalium: A sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by a bacterium of the same name; the condition may be asymptomatic or involve pain and vaginal or penile discharge and may cause infertility in women if left untreated. Trichomonad: A parasitic protozoan that often infects the urogenital and digestive systems; a trichomonad has an undulating membrane and four flagella (microscopic whiplike tails), which allow it to swim. Coupled with 17 other genetic biomarkers, the test can accurately predict the presence of high–grade prostate cancer. The procedure involves reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR), which uses RNA in the specimen as a template to make DNA (reverse transcription) and creates more copies of the DNA using PCR. The evaluation uses next generation sequencing (NGS), which uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. The procedure involves extracting circulating tumor cell–free DNA (cfDNA) from the plasma specimen to identify 59 markers that indicate the presence of pancreatic cancer. The markers are methylation haplotype blocks, which are closely bound cytosine and guanine bases connected by a phosphate group. The 59 markers indicate patterns in cfDNA indicating the presence of a pancreatic tumor or precancerous lesion. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Cell–free DNA (cfDNA): Nonencapsulated DNA in the form of nucleic acid fragments that enter the bloodstream during apoptosis (programmed, or normal, cell death) or necrosis (cell death due to loss of blood supply from injury, radiation, or chemicals). The lab analyst processes the sputum into a single–cell suspension with fluorescently–labeled porphyrin (TCPP) and antibodies that selectively bind to cancer cells and other cells of interest, as well as a dye for cell viability. Using the flow cytometry findings plus patient data such as age, the algorithm provides a score for the likelihood that the patient has lung cancer on a scale from 0.0 (very unlikely) to 1.0 (very likely). Clinicians may order this test for patients with suspicious findings on computed tomography (CT) testing. Explanation Using a direct nasal swab without viral transport media, the lab analyst performs the technical steps for qualitative detection of SARS–CoV–2 antigens. The reaction changes the resonance frequency of the bound protein, which the instrument detects using a bulk acoustic wave (BAW) biosensor. The frequency shift correlates with the concentration of SARS–CoV–2 viral antigens, and the test provides a result of “positive” or “negative” for SARS–CoV–2 antigens. short_description: Oncology (solid tumor), DNA (80 genes) and RNA (36 genes), by next-generation sequencing from plasma, including single nucleotide variants, insertions/deletions, copy number alterations, microsatellite instability, and fusions, report showing identified mutations with clinical actionability
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0409U only for LiquidHALLMARK® from Lucence Health Inc. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to evaluate circulating cell–free DNA and RNA from a plasma specimen for alterations to 80 and 36 genes, respectively, and reports any identified mutations along with a guide to possible clinically actionable treatment options. Explanation The lab analyst processes a patient plasma specimen to isolate circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and possibly ctRNA for analysis, which is a procedure sometimes called a liquid biopsy. The test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS), which uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. This test interrogates 80 DNA mutations for variants such as single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and insertions/deletions (indels) and 10 gene fusions. The test may also include analysis of 36 ctRNA targets. The mutations investigated are associated with 15 types of cancer, including breast, lung, and colon cancer. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Clinicians may order this test at any stage of a patient’s cancer development, from aiding in diagnosis and therapy selection to monitoring therapy response or detecting emergent mutations over time. Clinicians may specifically order this test as a noninvasive option to biopsy. short_description: Oncology (pancreatic), DNA, whole genome sequencing with 5-hydroxymethylcytosine enrichment, whole blood or plasma, algorithm reported as cancer detected or not detected
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0410U only for Avantect™ Pancreatic Cancer Test from ClearNote™ Health. The test uses 5–hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) biomarker profiling and whole–genome sequencing to evaluate a blood specimen from a patient at high risk of developing pancreatic cancer. The test may help identify pancreatic cancer in patients earlier than other common test methods and indicate a path for follow–up testing. Explanation The lab analyst processes a patient blood specimen to isolate cell–free DNA (cfDNA) for analysis, which is a procedure sometimes called a liquid biopsy. To identify signs present in the earliest stages of pancreatic cancer, the test includes whole genome sequencing and evaluation of 5–hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), which is a chemical modification of DNA that serves as a targeted biomarker of epigenomic changes (factors that impact gene expression). This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Because risk of developing pancreatic cancer increases significantly over age 50, especially in patients with new–onset type II diabetes, clinicians may order this test for patients in that risk category. The algorithmic analysis for this test provides a finding for possible pancreatic cancer as “signal detected,” which indicates the need for follow–up imaging tests such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). The finding of “signal not detected” may indicate the need for repeating the test, such as in six months. Cell–free DNA (cfDNA): Nonencapsulated DNA in the form of nucleic acid fragments that enter the bloodstream during apoptosis (programmed, or normal, cell death) or necrosis (cell death due to loss of blood supply from injury, radiation, or chemicals). Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Liquid biopsy: Blood test to find biomarkers or bits of nucleic acids or cancer cells that break off from a tumor and circulate in the blood; may be useful for finding early–stage cancer. Using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS), the test evaluates a plasma specimen for levels of beta amyloid 40 and 42, as well as identifying the patient’s apolipoprotein E (ApoE) protein phenotype (such as ApoE2 or ApoE4). The analyst also uses LC–MS/MS to identify the isoform (phenotype, or gene expression) of the protein, apolipoprotein E (ApoE), in the specimen, which correlates to the patient genotype. Clinicians may order this test for patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia as an early biomarker of Alzheimer’s disease. short_description: Oncology (hematolymphoid neoplasm), optical genome mapping for copy number alterations, aneuploidy, and balanced/complex structural rearrangements, DNA from blood or bone marrow, report of clinically significant alterations
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0413U only for DH Optical Genome Mapping/Digital Karyotyping Assay from The Clinical Genomics and Advanced Technology (CGAT) Laboratory at Dartmouth Health, and Bionano Genomics. The test uses optical genome mapping (OGM) to identify aneuploidy (chromosome mutation), copy number variations (CNVs), and complex structural DNA rearrangements implicated in hematolymphoid neoplasia, which are blood and bone–marrow cancers. Explanation The lab analyst uses the optical genome mapping (OGM) system from Bionano Genomics to isolate ultra–high molecular weight DNA and process the DNA with fluorescent labels. The system allows optical evaluation of the patient’s chromosomes for large scale changes in DNA, such as aneuploidy (chromosome mutation), copy number variations (CNVs), and complex structural DNA rearrangements. The single assay provides findings similar to what would otherwise require a combination of cytogenetic techniques such as karyotyping, chromosomal microarrays (CMAs), and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Clinicians may order this test to detect all relevant chromosomal aberrations that impact diagnosis and treatment of hematologic neoplasms such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), multiple myeloma (MM), plasma cell myeloma (PCM), chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), and more. Cytogenetics: Genetic studies related to structural variation of chromosomes. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH): A laboratory test in which a special stain that includes a DNA or RNA probe, which selectively attaches to a target segment of DNA or RNA, is applied to a tissue sample in situ hybridization (ISH); the probe includes some kind of marker, often a fluorescent molecule, which can be analyzed with a fluorescence microscope to detect and localize the target in the tissue (fluorescence ISH, or FISH); fluorescence describes a substance which absorbs and emits light. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Karyotyping: A lab test that pairs?all chromosomes of an organism to reveal number and structural features that could indicate genetic anomalies. Leukemia: A cancer of the blood cells, with various types named after the specific blood cell type that becomes cancerous; it almost always results in a great increase in white blood cells (leukocytes). Microarray: A lab device composed of a surface with a grid of dots containing different DNA sequences that act as probes to capture targets in the specimen; used to map gene expression; sometimes called a gene chip. Rearrangement: Alteration in gene sequence due to breakage and reattachment.? Translocation: The process or genetic abnormality that occurs when disparate portions of one or more chromosomes become attached and create a hybrid segment, known as a fusion gene, inserted in one or?both of the broken?chromosomes.? Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Report 0414U only for LungOI from Imagene. The test uses digitized pathology slides from formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) lung tumor tissue stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Using artificial intelligence (AI) with algorithms and bioinformatics databases, the test evaluates the slide for mutations in at least eight genes listed in the code and reports the findings as positive or negative for each. Explanation The analyst operates a computer system to input digitized pathology slides from formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) lung tumor tissue stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Using artificial intelligence (AI) with algorithms and bioinformatics databases for specific genetic mutations, tumor tissue images, and diagnoses, the test evaluates the slide for mutations in at least eight genes listed in the code. The test may also include evaluation for KRAS G12C and PD–L1 genes. Clinicians may order this test based on digitized slides from patient lung biopsy or excision specimens. The test allows rapid evaluation for key gene mutations that may aid in diagnosis and indication of treatment options without the delay of ordering genetic analysis tests that use more traditional methods such as next generation sequencing. Digital image: A picture converted to numerical data for storage and viewing on a computer.? Formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE): A method to preserve a tissue specimen, such as a biopsy, and prepare it for microscopic examination; the process uses formalin (formaldehyde) to preserve (fix) the tissue and paraffin to embed the tissue in a waxy block that can be sliced thin for viewing on a microscope slide.? Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein.? Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism.? Explanation Using a urine specimen, the lab analyst extracts exosomes (extracellular vesicles) that contain nucleic acids, then isolates 53 small noncoding RNAs (sncRNAs) that serve as biomarkers for prostate cancer. The analyst performs quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT–qPCR) to evaluate gene activity (expression). This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results, and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. Clinicians may order this test as a noninvasive urine test to evaluate a patient’s prostate cancer status and risk. Using the test results plus patient data in an algorithmic analysis, the test indicates the findings as no molecular evidence or low–, moderate–, or elevated–risk of prostate cancer. The test is a liquid biopsy that may allow clinicians to determine an appropriate surveillance or treatment protocol without repeat prostate specific antigen (PSA) tests, digital rectal exam (DRE), or invasive prostate biopsy. Reverse transcription: Generation of a complementary DNA sequence from a template of RNA. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. short_description: Glycine receptor alpha1 IgG, serum or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), live cell-binding assay (LCBA), qualitative
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Using a live–cell binding method, the test evaluates a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or serum specimen for the presence of immunoglobulin G (IgG) for alpha–1 subunit of glycine receptor, which is a biomarker for the autoimmune stiff–person spectrum of disorders. Explanation The lab analyst grows specific live cells that can encode alpha–1 subunit of glycine receptor in the presence of doxycycline (an antibiotic also used for lab purposes). Patient cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or serum is added to cell cultures with and without doxycycline. CSF or serum containing IgG specific for glycine receptor alpha–1 will be positive on cells with doxycycline, as evidenced by a fluorophore marker. Clinicians may order this test for patients with symptoms such as exaggerated startle, spasms, and stiffness of the limbs and/or core. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): A clear serum–like fluid that circulates in the ventricles of the brain and around the surface of the brain and spinal cord; it helps maintain uniform pressure within the spinal cord and brain. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Stiff person spectrum disorder (SPSD): A group of conditions characterized by startle, spasms, and stiffness of the limbs and/or trunk due to autoimmune antibodies. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0432U only for Kelch–Like Protein 11 Antibody from Mayo Clinic/Mayo Clinic Laboratories. Using a cell binding assay method, the test evaluates a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or serum specimen for the presence of Kelch–Like Protein 11 (KLHL11) Antibody, which is a biomarker for autoimmune or neoplasm–associated encephalitis. Explanation The lab analyst uses specific cultured cells encoded with Kelch–Like Protein 11 (KLHL11) and tagged with a fluorescent protein. short_description: Oncology, chemotherapeutic drug cytotoxicity assay of cancer stem cells (CSCs), from cultured CSCs and primary tumor cells, categorical drug response reported based on cytotoxicity percentage observed, minimum of 14 drugs or drug combinations
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0435U only for ChemoID® from ChemoID® Lab and Cordgenics LLC. Using bulk tumor cells and cultured cancer stem cells from a fresh tumor biopsy, the test is a drug–response assay for the cytotoxicity effect of a minimum of 14 chemotherapy drugs or drug combinations. Explanation Using a fresh tumor biopsy, the lab analyst cultures both bulk tumor cells and cancer stem cells (CSCs) in a medium unfavorable to normal stromal cells, and enriches the CSCs. The analyst exposes the cultured cells to at least 14 chemotherapy drugs or drug combinations and dosages specified by the oncologist. The test generates a prioritized list of effective and ineffective chemotherapies based on the percentage of tumor–derived cells and CSCs that are killed using each drug or their combinations. The response curve is presented graphically as a cytotoxic index. Cytotoxic means toxic to cells. The results help determine which chemotherapy agents or combinations will kill both bulk tumor cells and cancer stem cells that are known to cause recurrence of the cancer. The rationale behind this assay is that in the course of standard chemotherapy regimens, bulk tumor cells are destroyed while the more resistant cancer stem cells survive, which can result in recurrence of the cancer. Clinicians may order this test to customize a treatment regimen that will not only destroy the existing cancer, but also prevent recurrence. Culture: To cultivate the growth of bacteria or other organisms or tissue cells in an artificial medium prepared with specific nutrients and incubated under specific conditions to encourage reproduction and growth of specific types of cells. Stem cells: Immature (undifferentiated) cells that develop into a variety of other cells types. Stromal cells: Connective tissue cells, such as fibroblasts, of any organ that support the function of the parenchymal cells (functional as opposed to structural or support cells) of that organ. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0437U only for MindX One™ Blood Test — Anxiety, from MindX Sciences. The test uses a blood specimen for gene expression profiling of 15 genes and algorithmic analysis of the findings to report a predictive risk score for anxiety disorders. Explanation Using a blood specimen, the lab analyst uses a method such as microarray gene expression profiling to identify which biomarkers (15 target genes) are actively expressed, (transcribed to RNA and translated to a protein that performs some function in the body). The lab analyst first stabilizes, extracts, and amplifies RNA from the specimen, then uses microarray technology, which is a slide or plate printed with known DNA sequences that act as probes to detect and quantify complementary sequences from the patient specimen. This is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA), which includes the analytical services to produce test results and uses those results plus patient data for an algorithmic analysis that reports the findings as a probability or risk score. The test uses bioinformatics to report a predictive risk score for anxiety disorders. The results include an evaluation of which drug therapies might effectively treat the patient’s condition. Clinicians may order this test to aid in diagnosis of anxiety disorders and to help target and monitor patient response to treatment medications. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output. Anxiolytics: Drugs used to treat anxiety disorders, sometimes called anti–anxiety drugs. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store,?and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems.? Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information.? Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA m(RNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Reverse transcription: Generation of a complementary DNA sequence from a template of RNA. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. The methodology is quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and digital PCR. The test includes an algorithmic analysis to generate the results of detected or not detected for coronary heart disease (CHD). Explanation This code represents PrecisionCHD™ from Cardio Diagnostics Inc. The lab analyst uses a whole–blood specimen to analyze single–nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 10 genes (rs710987 [LINC010019], rs1333048 [CDKN2B–AS1], rs12129789 [KCND3], rs942317 [KTN1–AS1], rs1441433 [PPP3CA], rs2869675 [PREX1], rs4639796 [ZBTB41], rs4376434 [LINC00972], rs12714414 [TMEM18], and rs7585056 [TMEM18]) and DNA methylation markers in six genes (cg03725309 [SARS1], cg12586707 [CXCL1], cg04988978 [MPO], cg17901584 [DHCR24–DT], cg21161138 [AHRR], and cg12655112 [EHD4]). These are biomarkers of coronary heart disease (CHD). The procedure involves quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and digital PCR (dPCR). PCR is a technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence. The process indicates which DNA sequences are actively expressed, meaning translated to a protein that performs a function in the body. dPCR provides absolute quantification of target nucleic acids in the sample by partitioning the sample into thousands of independent fragments for testing. short_description: Infectious disease (bacterial, fungal, or viral infection), semiquantitative biomechanical assessment (via deformability cytometry), whole blood, with algorithmic analysis and result reported as an index
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0441U only for IntelliSep® test from Cytovale®. The test uses a whole–blood sample to assess a patient’s likelihood of developing sepsis. The method is semiquantitative biomechanical assessment (via deformability cytometry), which involves observing how cells deform under stress. The test includes an algorithmic analysis and reports the result as an index, categorizing the patient’s risk of developing sepsis. Explanation The lab analyst uses a whole–blood specimen to assess the likelihood of sepsis in a patient with signs and symptoms of infection. The method is semiquantitative biomechanical assessment via deformability cytometry, a technique used to measure the mechanical properties of cells. This method involves passing cells through a microfluidic channel, which is a tiny conduit designed to control and manipulate fluids at the microscale level. The test observes how the cells deform under stress. The degree of deformation can provide useful information because, when squeezed, cells from a healthy donor and cells from a patient with sepsis look different. This service includes the analytical services to produce test results and reports the result as an index, categorizing the patient’s risk of developing sepsis. Clinicians may order this test as part of evaluating a patient with signs and symptoms of an infection. The ordering provider can factor the results regarding the patient’s risk of developing sepsis into treatment and triage decisions. Sepsis is a potentially life–threatening condition caused by the body’s response to an infection. The body normally releases chemicals into the bloodstream to fight an infection. Sepsis occurs when the body’s response to these chemicals is out of balance, triggering changes that can damage multiple organ systems.
