lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0442U only for FebriDx® Bacterial/Non–Bacterial Point–of–Care Assay from Lumos Diagnostics LLC. The test uses a fingerstick whole–blood specimen to assess a patient with signs and symptoms of a respiratory infection to see if the source is bacterial. The test result indicates the presence or absence of the biomarkers Myxovirus resistance protein A (MxA) and C–reactive protein (CRP). Explanation The analyst uses a point–of–care device (meaning one used where the patient receives care, such as urgent care or an emergency room) to collect a drop of blood from a fingerstick. The test assesses a patient with signs and symptoms of a respiratory infection to see if the source is bacterial. When the blood collection tube of the device is full, the analyst follows the instructions for the particular device, typically laying the test device on a flat surface, releasing a buffer present in the device, and waiting a short time, such as 10 minutes, for the results to appear. The test result indicates the presence or absence of the biomarkers Myxovirus resistance protein A (MxA) and C–reactive protein (CRP). A typical device shows one line as a control line and then has space for two additional lines. A line that indicates MxA is interpreted to mean the source of the infection is not bacterial because MxA is specific for viral infection only. Infection stimulates CRP elevation, but it is nonspecific for the cause of the infection. Clinicians may order this test as part of evaluating a patient with signs and symptoms of a respiratory infection. The ordering provider can use the results to decide whether to prescribe antibiotics, which treat bacterial infections. Explanation The lab analyst evaluates DNA from a formalin fixed–paraffin–embedded tumor tissue sample using a next–generation sequencing (NGS) targeted gene panel. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes. Test results that identify specific translocations can help in the definitive diagnosis of various cancers. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0445U only for Elecsys® Phospho–Tau (181P) CSF (pTau181) and β–Amyloid (1–42) CSF II (Abeta 42) Ratio from Roche Diagnostics Operations Inc. The test uses cerebrospinal fluid for an electrochemiluminescent immunoassay (ECLIA) that generates a pTau181/Abeta42 ratio value, which may help the provider diagnose a patient with signs of cognitive impairment. Explanation The lab analyst performs an electrochemiluminescent immunoassay (ECLIA) test to measure the predictive biomarkers β–Amyloid (1–42) (Abeta42) and Phospho–Tau (181P) (pTau181) in cerebrospinal fluid. The lab analyst carries out multiple technical steps to process and test the specimen using immunoassay methods that include placing the specimens in the wells of an automated device, along with a chemiluminescent reagent that binds to the detection antibody only when activated by an electrical charge. The lab analyst runs the Abeta42 and pTau181 assays individually, and a system uses the individual results to calculate a pTau181/Abeta42 ratio value. A positive result, defined as a pTau181/Abeta42 ratio value above a defined cut–off, is consistent with a positive amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) scan result, which may be indicative of Alzheimer’s disease. Clinicians may order this test for patients being evaluated for Alzheimer’s disease and other causes of cognitive impairment. The provider can use the results in addition to other clinical diagnostic evaluations to diagnose the patient and develop treatment plans. Terminology Alzheimer's disease: A slowly progressive form of dementia characterized by beta–amyloid plaques (microscopic clumps of pieces of protein), tangles (strands) of the tau protein (abundant in the central nervous system but not elsewhere), brain inflammation, and damage and eventual death of brain cells. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin (Ig). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): A clear serum–like fluid that circulates in the ventricles of the brain and around the surface of the brain and spinal cord; it helps maintain uniform pressure within the spinal cord and brain. Cognitive: Referring to the brain's intellectual activity, such as thinking, remembering, or reasoning. Electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA): A laboratory testing method that uses the electrochemical properties of specific markers to produce light and identify a substance with a luminometer. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Positron emission tomography (PET): A nuclear medicine imaging technique that produces a three–dimensional image of functional processes in the body; the system detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron–emitting radionuclide (tracer), which is introduced into the body on a biologically active molecule (glucose). Reagent: A substance used in a lab test to bring about a desired change or reaction, often to reveal the presence or quantity of another substance that is the focus of the test. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Explanation Using a specimen, such as a blood specimen, the lab analyst performs a next–generation sequencing panel to evaluate at least five genes (CFTR, SMN1, HBB, HBA1, and HBA2). NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes. Clinicians may order this test to screen a patient to see if they are a carrier for severe inherited conditions. Examples include cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, beta hemoglobinopathies (including sickle cell disease), and alpha thalassemia. Terminology Alpha thalassemia: A blood disorder that reduces the production of hemoglobin (the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen to cells throughout the body); this condition is caused by mutations in the genes that help control the production of alpha globin, a component of hemoglobin; there are two main types of alpha thalassemia, which are distinguished by their severity: alpha thalassemia major, which is a very severe form of the disease, and alpha thalassemia minor, which is a milder form; symptoms can range from mild anemia to more severe health problems such as growth failure, bone abnormalities, and life–threatening complications. Atrophy: Reduction in the amount of tissue, which can be due to aging, malnourishment, or lack of exercise; loss of muscle bulk is an example of atrophy. Cystic fibrosis: An inherited disorder characterized by the production of thick, sticky mucus that blocks pancreatic ducts and clogs the lungs. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Sickle cell disease: A group of inherited red blood cell (RBC) disorders caused by an abnormal protein in the RBCs that gives the cells a curved sickle shape and results in RBC death with anemia and other complications. short_description: Oncology (bladder), methylated PENK DNA detection by linear target enrichment-quantitative methylation-specific real-time PCR (LTE-qMSP), urine, reported as likelihood of bladder cancer
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0452U only for EarlyTect® Bladder Cancer Detection (EarlyTect® BCD), Promis Diagnostics Inc. The test, on a urine specimen, uses linear target enrichment–quantitative methylation–specific real–time PCR (LTE–qMSP) for methylated PENK DNA detection. PENK methylation is a biomarker of bladder cancer, and the results are reported as the likelihood of bladder cancer. Explanation The lab analyst performs the steps necessary for linear target enrichment–quantitative methylation–specific real–time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which is a laboratory technique to study specific parts of DNA. The first step, linear target enrichment, isolates the specific segments of DNA that are of interest for the study. This helps to focus the study on just the necessary parts. The next part of the process involves quantitative methylation–specific analysis. This is a way of measuring the methylation of DNA, a process that can control how genes are activated or deactivated. The final part of the process is real–time PCR. This is a technique that makes many copies of a specific part of DNA, so there’s enough to study. This test involves detection of methylated PENK DNA. PENK stands for proenkephalin, which is a molecule that the body processes to produce small proteins called enkephalins. PENK methylation is a biomarker for bladder cancer. The results are reported as the likelihood of bladder cancer. Clinicians may order this test for patients with hematuria (blood in the urine) to determine the likelihood that the patient has bladder cancer. Terminology Real–time polymerase chain reaction (real–time PCR): A laboratory technique that monitors the progress of a PCR reaction in real time and allows quantification (counting) of PCR product (DNA, cDNA, or RNA) from a relatively small amount; sometimes called quantitative PCR (qPCR). Report 0453U only for ColonAiQ® from Breakthrough Genomics. The test is on a blood plasma specimen, which contains cell–free DNA (cfDNA), which includes circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) if cancer is present. The test uses a quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay to target certain genes that may undergo changes in their methylation patterns when colorectal cancer is present. The results indicate the presence or absence of circulating tumor DNA. Explanation The lab analyst performs the steps necessary for a methylation–based quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay on a plasma sample from the patient. The plasma sample contains cell–free DNA (cfDNA), which includes circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) if cancer is present. The lab uses methylation–based quantitative PCR assay to analyze this cfDNA. A PCR assay is a technique that amplifies a single or a few copies of a segment of DNA across several orders of magnitude, generating copies of a particular DNA sequence. This test specifically targets and amplifies certain genes, SEPTIN9, IKZF1, BCAT1, Septin9–2, VAV3, and BCAN, that may undergo changes in their methylation patterns when colorectal cancer is present. Methylation is a process that can turn genes on or off. The PCR assay amplifies these genes, making them easier to detect and analyze. The results of the test are then reported as either the presence or absence of ctDNA, indicating whether or not cancerous cells are present in the body. Methylation analysis: Analysis of DNA patterns following attachment of methyl groups to cytosine bases to indicate the presence or absence of genetic changes related to a disease. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0454U only for Chromosome Genome Mapping from UR Medicine Labs. The test, on a specimen such as blood, uses optical genome mapping (OGM) to identify chromosomal structural variants to aid in diagnosis of genetic disorders. Explanation The lab analyst performs optical genomic mapping (OGM), which offers a high–resolution view of the structural organization of chromosomes and DNA. OGM focuses on identifying and mapping structural variations in the genome, such as copy number variations, inversions, insertions, deletions, and translocations. The single assay provides similar data typically available using different assays, such as chromosomal microarray, Fragile X testing, and karyotyping. Clinicians may order this test to aid in diagnosis and treatment of patients with suspected genetic disorders. Terminology Chromosome: Found in the nucleus of cells, a chromosome is a DNA molecule that appears as a threadlike structure, especially during cell division; the chromosomes that determine the sex of an individual are called sex chromosomes; males have one Y and one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Duplication and/or deletion: Increase and/or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Fragile X syndrome: A genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the FMR1 gene, resulting in intellectual disability and certain facial characteristics. Heritable: Refers to the variance of a genetic trait as it's expressed in a population, i.e., a certain genetic trait be expressed 80% of the time, 60% of the time, or 30% of the time; inheritable simply means that a certain trait, such a color of eyes or hair, is genetic. Karyotyping: A lab test that pairs all chromosomes of an organism to reveal number and structural features that could indicate genetic anomalies. Rearrangement: Alteration in gene sequence due to breakage and reattachment. Translocation: The process or genetic abnormality that occurs when disparate portions of one or more chromosomes become attached and create a hybrid segment, known as a fusion gene, inserted in one or both of the broken chromosomes. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Infectious agents (sexually transmitted infection), Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis, multiplex amplified probe technique, vaginal, endocervical, gynecological specimens, oropharyngeal swabs, rectal swabs, female or male urine, each pathogen reported as detected or not detected
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0455U only for Abbott Alinity™ m STI Assay from Abbott Molecular Inc. The test evaluates vaginal swabs, endocervical swabs, gynecological specimens, oropharyngeal swabs, rectal swabs, female urine, or male urine using a multiplex amplified probe technique to detect Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis, which cause common sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Explanation The lab analyst processes the specimen, such as a vaginal swab, endocervical swab, gynecological specimen, oropharyngeal swab, rectal swab, or female or male urine, using an instrument. The automated system extracts DNA and uses reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR) to amplify (increase the number of) target genes to detect and differentiate Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis. The procedure uses multiplex probe technique (able to simultaneously evaluate multiple analytes in a single procedure) and reports the findings for each organism as detected or not detected. Clinicians may order this test for male or female patients exhibiting symptoms, such as pain, sores, odor, or discharge, of a sexually transmitted infection (STI). Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Explanation The lab analyst performs the steps necessary for liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) on a blood plasma or serum specimen. Plasma is the clear, yellowish liquid portion of blood, in which cells are suspended. Serum is the liquid portion of the blood that remains after the blood cells and clotting factors have been removed. LC–MS/MS is a laboratory technique that separates and identifies the components of a mixture. In this process, liquid chromatography first separates the mixture into its individual components. Then, the components are analyzed by mass spectrometry twice (hence the term tandem). The test determines the amount of nine perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). PFAS are man–made chemicals that have been used in industry and consumer products, such as nonstick cookware, carpets, and firefighting foams. short_description: ?-amyloid (Abeta42) and total tau (tTau), electrochemiluminescent immunoassay (ECLIA), cerebral spinal fluid, ratio reported as positive or negative for amyloid pathology
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0459U only for Elecsys® Total Tau CSF (tTau) and β–Amyloid (1–42) CSF II (Abeta 42) Ratio from Roche Diagnostics Operations Inc. The test uses cerebrospinal fluid for electrochemiluminescent immunoassay (ECLIA) tests that generate a tTau/Abeta42 ratio value, which may help the provider diagnose a patient with signs of cognitive impairment. Explanation The lab analyst performs electrochemiluminescent immunoassay (ECLIA) tests to measure the predictive biomarkers β–Amyloid (1–42) (Abeta42) and total Tau (tTau) in cerebrospinal fluid. The lab analyst carries out multiple technical steps to process and test the specimen using immunoassay methods that include placing the specimens in the wells of an automated device, along with a chemiluminescent reagent that binds to the detection antibody only when activated by an electrical charge. The lab analyst runs the Abeta42 and tTau assays individually, and a system uses the individual results to calculate a tTau/Abeta42 ratio value. A positive result, defined as a tTau/Abeta42 ratio value above a defined cutoff, is consistent with a positive amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) scan result, which may be indicative of Alzheimer’s disease. Clinicians may order this test for patients being evaluated for Alzheimer’s disease and other causes of cognitive impairment. The provider can use the results in addition to other clinical diagnostic evaluations to diagnose the patient and develop treatment plans. Terminology Alzheimer’s disease: A slowly progressive form of dementia characterized by beta–amyloid plaques (microscopic clumps of pieces of protein), tangles (strands) of the tau protein (abundant in the central nervous system but not elsewhere), brain inflammation, and damage and eventual death of brain cells. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin (Ig). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): A clear serum–like fluid that circulates in the ventricles of the brain and around the surface of the brain and spinal cord; it helps maintain uniform pressure within the spinal cord and brain. Cognitive: Referring to the brain's intellectual activity, such as thinking, remembering, or reasoning. Electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA): A laboratory testing method that uses the electrochemical properties of specific markers to produce light and identify a substance with a luminometer. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Positron emission tomography (PET): A nuclear medicine imaging technique that produces a three–dimensional image of functional processes in the body; the system detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron–emitting radionuclide (tracer), which is introduced into the body on a biologically active molecule (glucose). Reagent: A substance used in a lab test to bring about a desired change or reaction, often to reveal the presence or quantity of another substance that is the focus of the test. short_description: Oncology, whole blood or buccal, DNA single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping by real-time PCR of 24 genes, with variant analysis and reported phenotypes
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0460U only for RightMed® Oncology Gene Report from OneOme® LLC. This test uses a whole blood or buccal (cheek) swab specimen and involves DNA single–nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping of 24 genes. SNP genotyping identifies variations in single nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA. The test also reports phenotypes (observable traits) based on the analysis. Explanation The lab analyst prepares the whole blood sample or a buccal swab (from the cheek, inside the mouth). The analyst extracts the DNA from the sample and subjects it to single–nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping, which involves identifying variations in single nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA. The analyst performs this genotyping using real–time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), a technique that amplifies targeted DNA sequences and allows for the detection and quantification of specific genetic variations. The analyst uses the real–time PCR to analyze 24 specific genes. The results from the PCR are analyzed to identify any variants, or differences, in the genes compared to a reference sequence. The test also reports phenotypes (observable traits) based on the analysis. Clinicians may order this test for patients to gain insights into genes related to cancer and cancer therapy. Terminology Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Real–time polymerase chain reaction (real–time PCR): A laboratory technique that monitors the progress of a PCR reaction in real time and allows quantification (counting) of PCR product (DNA, cDNA, or RNA) from a relatively small amount; sometimes called quantitative PCR (qPCR). Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP): Compared to the population, a difference in a single nucleotide in a nucleic acid sequence that may be associated with a specific disease or condition. short_description: Oncology (cervix), mRNA gene expression profiling of 14 biomarkers (E6 and E7 of the highest-risk human papillomavirus [HPV] types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58), by real-time nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (NASBA), exo- or endocervical epithelial cells, algorithm reported as positive or negative for increased risk of cervical dysplasia or cancer for each biomarker
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0463U only for Proofer ‘7 HPV mRNA E6 and E7 Biomarker Test from Global Diagnostics Labs LLC and PreTect AS, a Mel–Mont Medical Inc. wholly owned subsidiary. Using a cervical specimen, the test evaluates gene activity (expression) of E6/E7 oncogenes. The test can identify overexpression of E6/E7, which indicates infection with one of the high–risk human papilloma virus (HPV) types and increased risk for cervical cancer. Explanation A lab analyst carries out a test related to cervical cancer, known as mRNA gene expression profiling. This test looks for 14 specific markers, including E6 and E7 from the most dangerous types of human papillomavirus (HPV), types 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58. The specimen is from the patient’s cervix. These can be either exocervical (from the outer surface of the cervix) or endocervical (from the inner surface or canal of the cervix) epithelial cells. Epithelial cells are a type of cell that line the surfaces of the body. These cells contain messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries genetic instructions from the DNA in the cell’s control center (nucleus) to the rest of the cell. The analyst uses a method called real–time nucleic acid sequence–based amplification (NASBA) to make many copies of the parts of the mRNA that match the 14 markers. This involves making a DNA copy (complementary DNA or cDNA) of the mRNA, and then using this cDNA as a pattern to make more copies of the original mRNA. The “real–time” part means that the making and detecting of the mRNA copies can be watched as it happens. Once the mRNA has been copied many times, the analyst can measure the amounts of each marker in the sample. This is done by comparing the amount of cDNA for each marker to a known reference amount. Finally, the results are analyzed using a special calculation process (algorithm), which decides whether the amounts of each marker suggest a higher risk of changes in the cervix (cervical dysplasia) or cervical cancer. The results are then reported as either positive or negative for each marker. Clinicians may order this test to help identify women at risk for cervical cancer. Over–production of E6/E7 indicates that the patient is infected with one of the listed high–risk HPV types, which is associated with an increased risk of developing cervical cancer. Terminology Cervical cancer: A type of cancer that develops from the cervix, a narrow passage that is part of the uterus; the cervix lies just above the vagina or the birth canal. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA (mRNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Human papillomavirus (HPV): Virus that causes warts on skin and mucous membranes in humans, especially genital warts; some papillomaviruses can cause cancer. Oncogene: A gene that can cause normal cells to change or mutate into abnormal or cancerous cells; oncogenes synthesize and regulate tumor–causing proteins called oncoproteins. short_description: Oncology (colorectal) screening, quantitative real-time target and signal amplification, methylated DNA markers, including LASS4, LRRC4 and PPP2R5C, a reference marker ZDHHC1, and a protein marker (fecal hemoglobin), utilizing stool, algorithm reported as a positive or negative result
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0464U only for Cologuard Plus™ from Exact Sciences Laboratories LLC. The test analyzes a stool sample for DNA markers (including LASS4, LRRC4 and PPP2R5C, and a reference marker ZDHHC1), as well as blood in the stool. It is a screening test for colorectal cancer. Abnormalities in genes LASS4, LRRC4, and PPP2R5C may indicate colorectal cancer. The results are analyzed using an algorithm, which determines whether the levels of each marker indicate an increased risk of colorectal cancer. The results are then reported as either a positive or negative result. Explanation A lab analyst carries out this colorectal cancer screening test by following several steps. The test uses a stool sample from the patient. This sample contains DNA, some of which may be methylated, meaning it has a small chemical tag added to it. Methylation can change the activity of a DNA segment without changing the sequence, and when it occurs in a certain pattern, it can be a sign of disease, including cancer. The analyst then prepares the sample for quantitative real–time target and signal amplification. This is a technique used to increase the amount of specific DNA segments in the sample, making them easier to detect and measure. In this case, the analyst is looking for methylated DNA markers, including LASS4, LRRC4, and PPP2R5C. These are genes that may be abnormally methylated in colorectal cancer. The analyst also checks for a reference marker, ZDHHC1, which helps to ensure the test is working correctly, and a protein marker, fecal hemoglobin (a protein in red blood cells), which can be a sign of bleeding in the digestive tract. Once the DNA has been amplified, the analyst measures the levels of each marker in the sample. This is done using a special machine that can detect and quantify the amplified DNA. Finally, the results are analyzed using an algorithm, which determines whether the levels of each marker indicate an increased risk of colorectal cancer. The results are then reported as either a positive or negative result. A positive result means the test found altered DNA and/or blood in the specimen. This indicates an increased risk of cancer, while a negative result means the markers do not indicate an increased risk. Clinicians may order this test to help screen patients for colorectal cancer. Terminology Methylation analysis: Analysis of DNA patterns following attachment of methyl groups to cytosine bases to indicate the presence or absence of genetic changes related to a disease. short_description: Oncology (urothelial carcinoma), DNA, quantitative methylation-specific PCR of 2 genes (ONECUT2, VIM), algorithmic analysis reported as positive or negative

The test analyzes a sample to detect specific DNA changes that involve methylation, a chemical modification, of two DNA markers (ONECUT2 and VIM). The results are then reported as either a positive or negative result. A positive result indicates the presence of these methylation markers and suggests a high risk of bladder cancer in the patient. Methylation is a biochemical process where a methyl group (a carbon and three hydrogen atoms) is added to the DNA, which can affect how genes are expressed. Abnormal methylation patterns can indicate the presence of cancer cells. The lab analyst performs PCR amplification, where the targeted DNA sequences are replicated multiple times to create enough material for accurate analysis. The test is quantitative, meaning the PCR allows the analyst to measure the amount of DNA amplified, providing an indication of how much methylated DNA is present. A computer algorithm analyzes the results from the PCR. This analysis determines whether the patterns of methylation observed are indicative of urothelial carcinoma. The final report from this test will state whether the result is positive or negative for the presence of cancer. A positive result indicates that the methylation markers associated with cancer are present, suggesting the patient is at high risk of having urothelial carcinoma. Clinicians may order this test for patients who have hematuria (blood in the urine) or bladder irritation to help in assessment for bladder cancer. short_description: Cardiology (coronary artery disease [CAD]), DNA, genome-wide association studies (564856 single-nucleotide polymorphisms [SNPs], targeted variant genotyping), patient lifestyle and clinical data, buccal swab, algorithm reported as polygenic risk to acquired heart disease
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0466U only for CardioRisk+ from Gene by Gene Ltd. and OpenDNA Ltd. The test analyzes DNA from a buccal (cheek) swab and combines the results with patient lifestyle and clinical data to perform algorithmic analysis. It is reported as polygenic risk to acquired heart disease, meaning the individual’s genetic susceptibility to heart disease. Explanation A lab analyst processes a buccal swab (taken from the cheek, inside the mouth) to examine specific genetic markers known as single–nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). SNPs are variations at a single position in DNA among individuals which may be linked to certain diseases, including coronary artery disease. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0469U only for IriSight™ CNV Analysis from Variantyx Inc. This is a genetic test for rare diseases, involving whole genome sequence analysis on fetal samples. The analysis detects various types of chromosomal abnormalities. The diagnostic report integrates these findings and compares them against maternal and paternal samples, if available, to aid in the identification and categorization of genetic variants, taking into account potential maternal cell contamination. Explanation The lab analyst undertakes a detailed process using whole genome sequence analysis of a fetal sample, which may include amniotic fluid, chorionic villus samples, or products of conception. Whole genome sequence analysis decodes the complete DNA sequence of an individual’s genome, which includes all of its genes and the regions that regulate gene expression. This is a lab test focused on rare diseases, particularly constitutional or heritable (genetically inherited) disorders. Constitutional, in this context, implies that the genetic abnormality is a fundamental part of the individual’s constitution and is present in the cells throughout the body. The analysis particularly targets chromosomal abnormalities such as copy number variants (abnormalities in the number of copies of a particular gene), duplications (repetitions of a segment of the chromosome), deletions (loss of a segment of the chromosome), inversions (where a chromosome segment breaks off, flips, and reattaches), unbalanced translocations (where parts of chromosomes are rearranged and reattached to other chromosomes but not in a balanced way), and regions of homozygosity (ROH; areas of the genome where the genetic material inherited from both parents is identical). Additionally, the test assesses inheritance patterns to detect uniparental disomy (UPD), where a child inherits two copies of a chromosome, or part of a chromosome, from one parent and none from the other. The presence of aneuploidy, an abnormal number of chromosomes, is also screened. The DNA from the sample is sequenced comprehensively, allowing the analyst to identify these genetic variances. The sequence data is then analyzed and compared against reference genomes to pinpoint any deviations indicative of disorders. If maternal and paternal samples are available, they are used as comparators to help distinguish inherited variations from new mutations and to check for maternal cell contamination in the fetal sample. Finally, the results are compiled into a diagnostic report that categorizes the genetic variants and correlates them with possible phenotypes (observable physical and biological characteristics) helping to guide clinical decisions regarding the presence and treatment of heritable disorders. Clinicians may order this test to assess a fetus, such as when a structural abnormality has been detected by ultrasound. The test helps identify chromosomal abnormalities associated with symptoms manifested in a fetus or a pregnancy, that may result in pregnancy loss or that cause severe, early–onset genetic disorders. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0470U only for HPV–SEQ Test from Sysmex Inostics Inc. In this oncology test for oropharyngeal cancer, the focus is on detecting minimal residual disease through next–generation sequencing (NGS). The test quantitatively evaluates eight specific DNA targets in cell–free human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 DNA extracted from a patient’s plasma. This highly sensitive technique helps in assessing the presence of very small amounts of cancerous cells remaining after treatment. Explanation The lab analyst uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) in this oncology lab test designed for oropharyngeal cancer to detect minimal residual disease, which refers to the very small number of cancer cells that may remain in the body after treatment and potentially lead to recurrence. The test specifically targets cell–free DNA (cfDNA) from human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18, which are commonly associated with oropharyngeal cancers. cfDNA refers to DNA fragments that are released into the bloodstream from cells undergoing apoptosis (programmed cell death) or necrosis (cell death caused by injury or disease). These DNA fragments are not contained within cells; instead, they freely circulate in the blood plasma, hence the term “cell–free.” These DNA fragments are isolated from a plasma sample, which is the liquid component of blood, collected from the patient. The process begins with the extraction of cfDNA from the plasma. Once extracted, the cfDNA is prepared for sequencing, a step that includes amplifying the DNA to ensure there is enough material for analysis. The NGS platform is then employed to quantitatively evaluate eight specific DNA targets linked to the HPV types. This technology allows for a highly sensitive and precise measurement of these genetic markers, enabling the detection of even minimal amounts of residual disease. The quantitative data obtained from NGS is analyzed to determine the presence and amount of residual HPV DNA in the plasma. The results are compiled into a detailed report for clinical use. Clinicians may order this test to assess treatment response, determine whether less intense treatment is appropriate, and monitor patients after treatment. short_description: Oncology (colorectal cancer), qualitative real-time PCR of 35 variants of KRAS and NRAS genes (exons 2, 3, 4), formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE), predictive, identification of detected mutations
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0471U only for CRCdx® RAS Mutation Detection Kit from EntroGen Inc. This oncology test for colorectal cancer uses qualitative real–time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect 35 specific variants of the KRAS and NRAS genes located in exons 2, 3, and 4. The sample used for this test is formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue, which preserves cancer tissue samples for detailed genetic examination. Explanation In this oncology test for colorectal cancer, the lab analyst conducts a qualitative real–time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect specific mutations in the KRAS and NRAS genes, focusing on exons 2, 3, and 4. These genes are known to play critical roles in cell signaling pathways that control cell growth and death, and mutations in these areas can influence the behavior of cancer cells and the effectiveness of targeted therapies. The test uses formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue samples, a common method where tissue is preserved in formalin and embedded in paraffin wax to maintain cellular details and structure for long–term study. To begin the test, the analyst first extracts DNA from the FFPE tissue samples. This involves cutting thin sections of the embedded tissue, deparaffinizing to remove the wax, and then using chemical treatments to release and purify the DNA. Once the DNA is extracted, the real–time PCR technique is applied. This method amplifies the target DNA sequences of the KRAS and NRAS genes to make them abundant enough for analysis. Real–time PCR allows the analyst to monitor the amplification process in real time with the use of fluorescent markers, which bind to the DNA and emit light if the target mutations are present. The outcome of the PCR provides qualitative data indicating whether the mutations are present in the genes studied, without quantifying the amount of mutated DNA. Identifying these mutations is predictive; it helps oncologists determine the likelihood of a patient responding to specific cancer therapies that target these mutations. This test uses enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to measure immunoglobulin G (IgG), immunoglobulin M (IgM), and immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies against three specific proteins: carbonic anhydrase VI (CA VI), parotid specific/secretory protein (PSP), and salivary protein (SP1). The test is performed on a blood sample and is semiqualitative, providing a positive or negative result based on the presence of these antibodies. The presence of these antibodies is reported as predictive evidence of early Sjögren’s syndrome, an autoimmune disorder that primarily affects the salivary and lacrimal glands, leading to dry mouth and dry eyes. Explanation A lab analyst uses the enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) technique on a blood sample to detect antibodies in the blood that may indicate early Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disorder. Specifically, the analyst measures the levels of immunoglobulin G (IgG), immunoglobulin M (IgM), and immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibodies targeting three proteins: carbonic anhydrase VI (CA VI), parotid specific/secretory protein (PSP), and salivary protein (SP1). These proteins are associated with salivary function, and antibodies against them can be a sign of autoimmune activity affecting the salivary glands. The analyst prepares the sample. The ELISA procedure involves coating a microplate with antigens, specifically, the proteins CA VI, PSP, and SP1. The patient’s prepared sample is added to the microplate; if the target antibodies (IgG, IgM, IgA) are present, they will bind to the respective antigens. After the binding, a secondary antibody that is enzyme–linked and specific to human IgG, IgM, or IgA is added, which binds to the complex of the antigen and primary antibody. A substance is then added that reacts with the enzyme, causing a measurable color change. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0473U only for xT CDx from Tempus AI Inc. This test uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to analyze the DNA of 648 genes from a solid tumor sample, which is preserved using formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) techniques. The tumor DNA is compared against DNA from a normal specimen (either blood or saliva) to detect genetic differences such as sequence variants, insertions and deletions, copy number variants, and rearrangements. Additionally, the test assesses microsatellite instability and calculates the tumor mutation burden, providing comprehensive insights into the tumor’s genetic landscape. Explanation To perform this oncology test for solid tumors, using next–generation sequencing (NGS) on DNA from formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) tissue, a lab analyst begins by preparing the tissue sample. The FFPE process preserves tissue samples by fixing them in a preservative solution of formalin and embedding them in paraffin wax, which stabilizes the DNA for long–term storage and subsequent analysis. The analyst extracts DNA from these tissues and also uses a matched normal specimen, which could be either blood or saliva. This normal specimen serves as a control to help identify genetic changes specific to the tumor. Once the DNA is extracted from both the tumor and normal samples, the analyst sequences all 648 genes using NGS. This technology allows for the rapid sequencing of DNA, enabling comprehensive analysis across multiple genes simultaneously. The test specifically interrogates for sequence variants, which are changes in the DNA sequence; insertion and deletion alterations, where DNA segments are added or removed; copy number variants, which involve changes in the number of copies of a particular gene; and rearrangements, where the DNA structure is altered. Additionally, the test evaluates for microsatellite instability, a condition where repeat DNA sequences become unstable and vary in length, and tumor–mutation burden, which measures the number of mutations within a tumor genome (complete set of genetic material, including DNA, that is present within the cells of a tumor). Comparative sequence analysis between the tumor and matched normal specimen allows the analyst to differentiate between inherited genetic variations and those specific to the cancer cells. Report 0474U only for GeneticsNow® Comprehensive Germline Panel from GoPath Diagnostics Inc. This test is a hereditary pan–cancer genomic sequence analysis that examines a panel of 88 genes associated with various inherited cancer syndromes, such as sarcomas, endocrine tumors, neuroendocrine tumors, and cutaneous melanoma. It employs next–generation sequencing (NGS) and Sanger sequencing to detect both sequence variants and 20 specific duplications or deletions in the genes, using either blood or saliva samples. The results are reported as positive or negative for each gene tested, indicating the presence or absence of germline variants that could predispose individuals to cancer. Explanation To perform the hereditary pan–cancer genomic sequence analysis, a lab analyst prepares a blood or saliva sample from the patient. This sample provides the DNA necessary for testing. The test specifically targets a panel of 88 genes associated with various types of hereditary cancers, including sarcomas, endocrine tumors, neuroendocrine tumors, and cutaneous melanoma. The analyst uses two primary sequencing techniques: next–generation sequencing (NGS) and Sanger sequencing. NGS allows for rapid, high–throughput sequencing of multiple genes simultaneously, making it efficient for scanning all 88 genes for mutations. In contrast, Sanger sequencing, a more traditional method, is typically used to confirm findings from NGS or to analyze specific areas of the genome with greater accuracy. The test focuses on identifying both sequence variants and specific structural changes within the DNA, namely 20 targeted duplications and deletions. Duplications mean that a segment of DNA is abnormally copied multiple times, and deletions refer to sections of DNA that are missing. These changes can significantly affect gene function and contribute to cancer risk. After sequencing, the data are analyzed to detect these genetic alterations. Each gene in the panel is assessed individually, and the results are reported as positive or negative for germline variants. Germline variants are genetic changes that are inherited and present in every cell of the body. Clinicians may order this test because identifying germline variants helps to determine an individual’s risk of developing cancer. The results can help clinicians provide guidance to patients about clinical risk and genetic causes of diseases. Examples of hereditary cancers include sarcomas, endocrine tumors, neuroendocrine tumors, and cutaneous melanoma. Sarcomas are cancers that start in the bones and soft tissues. Endocrine tumors form in the endocrine glands, which are responsible for hormone production. Neuroendocrine tumors develop from cells that share characteristics of both hormone–producing and nerve cells, and they can occur in various organs. Cutaneous melanoma, a type of skin cancer, originates from melanocytes, the cells that give skin its color. This cancer has the potential to spread rapidly to other parts of the body. short_description: Autoinflammatory disease (VEXAS syndrome), DNA, UBA1 gene mutations, targeted variant analysis (M41T, M41V, M41L, c.118-2A>C, c.118-1G>C, c.118-9_118-2del, S56F, S621C)
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0500U only for QClamp® Plex VEXAS UBA1 Mutation Test from DiaCarta Inc. This test detects specific mutations in the UBA1 gene using targeted variant analysis to diagnose VEXAS syndrome. Explanation This code represents QClamp® Plex VEXAS UBA1 Mutation Test from DiaCarta Inc. For this test, the lab analyst processes a DNA sample to detect specific mutations in the UBA1 gene (M41T, M41V, M41L, c.118–2A>C, c.118–1G>C, c.118–9_118–2del, S56F, S621C). These mutations are associated with VEXAS syndrome, which stands for vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X–linked, autoinflammatory, somatic syndrome. It is a chronic, progressive disease that causes severe systemic anti–inflammatory and hematological symptoms, including skin rashes that may be painful and swelling, and pain in nose and ears (nose and/or ear chondritis), cough and shortness of breath, pain and swelling in joints, inflammation of blood vessels, and failure of the bone marrow (e.g., macrocytic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome). It is a rare autoinflammatory disease. short_description: Reproductive medicine (preimplantation genetic assessment), analysis of 24 chromosomes using DNA genomic sequence analysis from embryonic trophectoderm for structural rearrangements, aneuploidy, and a mitochondrial DNA score, results reported as normal/balanced (euploidy/balanced), unbalanced structural rearrangement, monosomy, trisomy, segmental aneuploidy, or mosaic, per embryo tested
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0553U only for Smart PGT–A Plus from Igenomix®, part of Vitrolife Group™, and Thermo Fisher Scientific. This test assesses in vitro fertilization (IVF) embryos for chromosomal abnormalities before implantation. A sample of the trophectoderm (from the outer layer of cells in the embryo) is tested for 24 chromosomes to detect issues such as structural rearrangements, extra or missing chromosomes, and mosaicism. It also provides a mitochondrial DNA score. Results indicate whether the embryo has normal chromosomes or specific abnormalities. Explanation This code represents Smart PGT–A Plus from Igenomix®, part of Vitrolife Group™, and Thermo Fisher Scientific. The lab uses a sample from the embryo’s trophectoderm (from the outer layer of cells in the embryo) and performs DNA sequence analysis on all 24 chromosomes. The test detects structural rearrangements (changes in the arrangement of chromosome segments), aneuploidy (extra or missing chromosomes), and mosaicism (a mixture of normal and abnormal cells in the embryo). A mitochondrial DNA score is also included. Mitochondria are small structures inside cells that produce energy, and each mitochondrion contains its own DNA. The amount of DNA may reflect whether the embryo is likely to implant and develop. Each embryo tested will have its results reported using specific categories. A result of normal/balanced (euploidy/balanced) means the embryo has the correct number of chromosomes. The term euploidy refers to having a normal number of chromosomes. Balanced indicates there is not any missing or extra genetic material. An unbalanced structural rearrangement indicates a chromosome change that causes a gain or loss of genetic material, which may impact development. Monosomy means one chromosome from a pair is missing, while trisomy means there is an extra chromosome, resulting in three copies instead of the usual two. Segmental aneuploidy refers to a missing or extra segment of a chromosome, rather than the whole chromosome. A result of mosaic means that different cells within the same embryo have different chromosome makeups. Some may be normal, while others may carry abnormalities. Clinicians may order this test for in vitro fertilization (IVF) embryos to identify embryos with the best chance of successful implantation and healthy development. lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0567U only for Genomic Unity® 2.0 from Variantyx Inc. It analyzes samples from blood, saliva, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, or tissue. Explanation This code represents Genomic Unity® 2.0 from Variantyx Inc. For this rare disease genetic test, the lab performs whole–genome sequencing, reading the complete DNA sequence using both short reads (small fragments) and long reads (larger fragments) to capture as much genetic information as possible. The test detects single–nucleotide variants (changes in a single building block of DNA), insertions and deletions (small pieces of DNA added or missing), characterized intronic variants (changes in noncoding regions of genes that can still impact gene function), copy–number variants (extra or missing sections of DNA), duplications and deletions (gains or losses of DNA segments), mobile element insertions (pieces of DNA that move around within the genome), runs of homozygosity (long stretches of identical DNA that can suggest consanguinity or inherited conditions), aneuploidy (an abnormal number of chromosomes), and inversions (segments of DNA that are reversed). It also sequences mitochondrial DNA, the genetic material found in the cell’s energy–producing structures, and detects mitochondrial deletions. Short tandem repeat genes, which contain repeating sequences, are analyzed, and methylation status of certain regions is assessed to identify abnormalities that may affect gene activity. Samples for testing may come from blood, saliva, amniotic fluid (amniocentesis), chorionic villus samples (from placental tissue), or other tissue. It measures levels of beta amyloid (Aβ40 and Aβ42), their ratio, phosphorylated tau protein (such as pTau217), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) using an ultrasensitive molecular array. The result is reported as positive, intermediate, or negative for Alzheimer’s pathology. Explanation This code represents LucentAD™ Complete from Quanterix Corporation. The test uses a plasma sample (the liquid portion of blood) to analyze several proteins that are associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Beta amyloid proteins (Aβ40 and Aβ42) are fragments found in the brain that can form plaques in people with Alzheimer’s. The test calculates the Aβ42/40 ratio, which can help assess the risk of plaque buildup. The test uses a highly sensitive technique to measure these proteins at very low levels. An algorithm evaluates the combination of these results and gives a report of positive, intermediate, or negative for Alzheimer’s pathology (physical changes that are characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease). Clinicians may order this test to help detect Alzheimer’s disease and guide diagnostic decisions for patients with memory or cognitive symptoms. short_description: Infectious disease (tropical fever pathogens), vector-borne and zoonotic pathogens, including 2 viruses (Chikungunya virus and Dengue virus serotypes 1, 2, 3, and 4), 1 bacterium (Leptospira species), and 1 parasite with species differentiation (Plasmodium species, Plasmodium falciparum, and Plasmodium vivax/ovale), real-time RT-PCR, whole blood, each pathogen reported as detected or not detected

This test analyzes a sample of whole blood using real–time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR) to detect multiple pathogens that cause tropical diseases. It identifies viruses, bacteria, and parasites that may be transmitted by insects or animals. Each result shows whether the pathogen is present or not. Explanation This code represents Biofire® Filmarray® Tropical Fever (TF) Panel from bioMérieux. The test is performed on a sample of whole blood to detect the presence of multiple pathogens that are commonly found in tropical regions and can be transmitted by mosquitoes (vector–borne) or animals (zoonotic). The test determines whether each pathogen is present in the sample and reports each one as either detected or not detected. short_description: Neurology (Alzheimer disease), plasma, 3 distinct isoform-specific peptides (APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4) by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), reported as an APOE prototype
lay_term: This is a Proprietary Laboratory Analyses (PLA) code, meaning that the code applies to only one unique lab test made by a specific manufacturer or performed by a specific lab. Report 0596U only for Precivity–ApoE™ from C2N Diagnostics LLC. This blood test detects three different forms of the APOE protein (APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4) using liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry. The results are summarized into an APOE proteotype to assist in assessing a person’s genetic profile related to Alzheimer's disease. Explanation This code represents Precivity–ApoE™ from C2N Diagnostics LLC. For this test, the lab analyst separates a blood sample for analysis. The laboratory uses a technique called liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) to measure three specific isoforms (or protein versions) of apolipoprotein E (APOE): APOE2, APOE3, and APOE4. Liquid chromatography is used to separate the components of the sample, while mass spectrometry identifies and measures the different APOE proteins based on their mass and structure. APOE is a protein involved in fat metabolism and is produced based on the APOE gene. Different isoforms of APOE are linked to different levels of risk for developing Alzheimer's disease. APOE4 is associated with higher risk, APOE2 may reduce risk, and APOE3 is considered neutral. Each person inherits two copies of the APOE gene, one from each parent, and the combination of these determines their APOE status. The test result is reported as an APOE proteotype, which reflects the specific combination of APOE isoforms present (for example, APOE3/APOE4 or APOE2/APOE3). This information provides insight into the person’s genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease. Clinicians may order this test to help assess a patient’s genetic risk for Alzheimer disease, particularly when evaluating cognitive symptoms or planning personalized approaches to care.
